In addition, registry definitions of ICP typically do not provide individual bile acid concentrations or longitudinal bile acid trajectories, and often lack information on bile acid composition and treatment exposure, which limits evaluation of biochemical severity, dose response patterns, and potentially modifiable pathways. Broader validation across healthcare systems, together with standardized developmental assessments beyond diagnostic codes, would improve phenotype resolution and strengthen causal inference [ , , , ]. These registry-level constraints highlight the need for more granular exposure characterization. Maternal bile acid concentrations vary across gestation and may change with treatment. A frequent limitation in many datasets is incomplete information on UDCA timing, dose, and adherence, which complicates interpretation of TBA trajectories. Future cohorts should record treatment initiation and pair these data with longitudinal bile acid measurements to better separate disease severity from treatment-related changes. Single-time-point measurements may therefore fail to capture cumulative exposure, critical windows of vulnerability, or bile acid composition. Longitudinal bile acid trajectories, bile acid species profiling, and linkage to placental transporter expression would help clarify dose–response relationships and timing-sensitive vulnerability [ , , ]. Human data showing altered fetal–maternal gradients and transplacental passage further support the feasibility of exposure assessment across maternal and fetal compartments in cohorts with detailed phenotyping [ ]. Mechanistic inference would benefit from models that better reflect pregnancy biology. The most coherent ICP pathway begins with altered fetal exposure and placental dysfunction [ – , ], but downstream fetal brain endpoints are still rarely tested directly in gestational models. Integrating injury programs centered on the placenta into animal models that reflect pregnancy biology, or into advanced placental–fetal experimental systems could enable direct testing of fetal brain endpoints [ – ]. Recent molecular studies implicating ferroptosis and epithelial–mesenchymal transition-related processes provide a mechanistic basis for this approach, allowing evaluation of microglial maturation, blood–brain barrier integrity, and neurobehavioral phenotypes across development [ , , , , ]. Treatment effects and long-term follow-up remain another major gap. While UDCA improves maternal symptoms and biochemistry, its effects on perinatal endpoints vary across study designs [ , ], and experimental data support actions on placental bile acid handling and vascular responses [ ]. Long-term follow-up of existing trial cohorts, alongside carefully designed observational studies capturing treatment timing and bile acid species, would help determine whether modifying maternal bile acid profiles translates into differences in later neurodevelopment [ , ]. A more integrated maternal–placental–offspring framework is likely to be most informative. Placental biology is central to developmental programming, and conceptual models that link placental dysfunction to offspring health later in life provide a useful scaffold for studies in ICP [ , , ]. Multidisciplinary studies that integrate obstetric exposure metrics with placental profiling, umbilical cord blood biomarkers, and standardized neurodevelopmental assessments in children will be critical for identifying subgroups most likely to benefit from targeted surveillance or early intervention. Conclusion In summary, ICP may not be confined to perinatal risks alone. An expanding body of population-based research suggests that intrauterine exposure to ICP may be associated with offspring outcomes beyond the neonatal period, including a higher risk of childhood neurodevelopmental diagnoses and measurable differences in early growth trajectories. Although the neurodevelopmental evidence is derived largely from Nordic registry studies, and observational designs cannot establish causality, these consistent signals support consideration of a life-course perspective when considering ICP. From a mechanistic standpoint, a pregnancy-specific sequence involving increased maternal bile acid burden, disrupted placental bile acid transport and handling, and consequent elevation of fetal exposure offers a coherent biological rationale for long-term effects. Placental inflammation, ER stress, oxidative stress, and vascular dysfunction may further shape the intrauterine environment during sensitive windows of brain development. Key priorities for future work include external validation in diverse populations, ideally through prospective cohorts. This should be coupled with refined exposure assessment that integrates longitudinal bile acid dynamics and profiles, placental and umbilical cord blood biomarkers, and mechanistic models that reflect pregnancy biology, to identify critical windows of exposure and potentially modifiable pathways. Such efforts will be essential to support evidence-based counseling and to guide long-term follow-up strategies for offspring exposed to ICP.

chunks.content: BACKGROUND Down syndrome (DS) is the most common genetic abnormality observed in newborns [ ]. Invasive diagnostic procedures such as chorionic villus sampling (CVS) and amniocentesis are recommended for high-risk populations, particularly women over the age of 35 or those with positive screening results. However, these procedures carry a procedure-related fetal loss risk of approximately 0.5% to 1% [ ]. Therefore, before resorting to invasive testing, ultrasound-based screening programs or cell-free DNA (cfDNA) tests may be preferred. Although cfDNA testing is available in many countries, its widespread use is limited due to high costs [ ]. Prenatal sonography has played an important role in the detection of fetuses with Down syndrome by identifying various sonographic markers. Currently, one of the most widely used and effective approaches for trisomy 21 screening involves the combination of maternal age, fetal nuchal translucency (NT), and maternal serum levels of free β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) and pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) measured between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation. This strategy has been reported to achieve detection rates approaching 90%, with a false-positive rate around 5% in some studies [ ]. It has also been estimated that incorporating the assessment of the fetal nasal bone (presence or absence) into the first-trimester combined screening can increase the detection rate up to 97% [ ]. Recent studies have indicated that the nasal bone is absent in approximately 64% of fetuses with Down syndrome during the first trimester, compared to around 4.8% in euploid fetuses. These findings suggest that nasal bone absence may serve as a useful adjunctive sonographic marker in early screening [ , ]. In the first trimester, evaluating the nasal bone may be challenging due to technical and developmental factors, as illustrated by data showing that 8.7% of nasal bones were initially absent or unclear. However, follow-up scans demonstrated the presence of nasal bones in over 71% of these cases, indicating that early non-visualization does not necessarily reflect a true absence [ ]. In contrast, nasal bone assessment during the second trimester is generally more feasible and reliable, making it a practical component of mid-trimester Down syndrome screening protocols [ ]. Moreover, hypoplastic nasal bone is not only associated with increased risk for trisomy 21, but may also be linked to a broader spectrum of genetic abnormalities detectable through chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), underscoring its relevance in comprehensive prenatal evaluation [ , ]. Second-trimester reference ranges for nasal bone length (NBL) have been reported for various populations, including Caucasian, African-American, South American, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Iranian fetuses [ ]. These studies indicate that ethnicity may influence the effectiveness of nasal bone screening for trisomy 21. However, establishing a definitive cutoff value for nasal bone hypoplasia remains challenging due to inter-ethnic variability [ , ]. Similarly, population-specific nomograms have also been reported in Turkish cohorts. Yanık et al. [ ] established normal second-trimester NBL reference ranges, while Göynümer et al. [ ] demonstrated gestational age–specific distributions in a large Turkish population. These findings emphasize that locally derived standards may improve diagnostic precision and reduce false-positive rates compared with universally applied thresholds. However, most previous Turkish studies primarily focused on normative measurements rather than evaluating the diagnostic performance of combined indices such as BPD/NBL ratio or NBL-MoM -based approaches. Given these findings, there is a growing interest in refining nasal bone measurements and related sonographic indices during the second trimester to improve the accuracy and clinical utility of prenatal screening. Accordingly, this study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of fetal nasal bone length (NBL), the biparietal diameter to nasal bone length ratio (BPD/NBL), and nasal bone length multiples of the median (NBL-MoM) values for Down syndrome (DS) screening between 17 and 25 weeks of gestation in a population-specific cohort. Methods This retrospective study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The medical records of pregnant women who underwent second-trimester ultrasound screening between 2011 and 2022 were reviewed. Written informed consent had been obtained from all participants. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ankara University Ethics Committee (approval number: 2025/696; date: 03 September 2025). All cases with a confirmed genetic diagnosis of Down syndrome during the second trimester between September 2011 and September 2022 constituted our study group. A total of 35 cases of Down syndrome were identified in this group. The control group included cases that underwent routine mid-trimester (17–25 weeks) ultrasound evaluation as part of clinical follow-up, delivered at our clinic, and had no structural or chromosomal abnormalities. Euploid status was confirmed by normal postnatal outcomes and the absence of phenotypic abnormalities at birth. This group included a total of 3070 cases. To ensure randomization, cases were randomly selected in equal distribution across each month within the study period. Gestational age was determined according to the last menstrual period (LMP)

September 2022 constituted our study group. A total of 35 cases of Down syndrome were identified in this group. The control group included cases that underwent routine mid-trimester (17–25 weeks) ultrasound evaluation as part of clinical follow-up, delivered at our clinic, and had no structural or chromosomal abnormalities. Euploid status was confirmed by normal postnatal outcomes and the absence of phenotypic abnormalities at birth. This group included a total of 3070 cases. To ensure randomization, cases were randomly selected in equal distribution across each month within the study period. Gestational age was determined according to the last menstrual period (LMP) and confirmed with ultrasonographic measurements during the first and second trimesters. Crown-rump length (CRL) in the first trimester and biparietal diameter (BPD) in the second trimester were used as reference. When the discrepancy between the LMP and ultrasonographic dating was more than 7 days in the first trimester or 14 days in the second trimester, ultrasound measurements were considered definitive; otherwise, the LMP was used. BPD and nasal bone lenght (NBL) measurements were recorded for all cases in both groups. Nasal bone measurements were performed in a true midsagittal section of the fetal head that visualized the nasal bone, lips, maxilla, and mandible, with the insonation angle positioned at approximately 45° or 135° relative to the nasal bone. For the control group, the median, 2.5th, 5th, 95th, and 97.5th percentiles of NBL measurements were calculated. BPD/NBL ratios were also computed. To calculate multiples of the median, each nasal bone length measurement was expressed as a nasal bone length multiple of the median (NBL-MoM), defined as the observed NBL divided by the expected gestational age–specific median derived from the control group. Log10 transformation was applied only for regression modelling and smoothing of the median curve. NBL-MoM calculations were performed using raw (non-transformed) measurements. Initially, we assessed whether the absence of the fetal nasal bone could predict DS. Subsequently, to evaluate hypoplasia independently of absence, additional analyses were performed in fetuses with a detectable nasal bone (NBL > 0). Then, among cases with detectable nasal bones, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of different cut-off values: NBL < 2.5 mm, < 2.5th and <5th percentiles, BPD/NBL ratios > 7.6, 8.5, 9, 10, 11, and 12, and NBL-MoM values < 0.65, < 0.75, < 0.76, and < 0.80. Statistical analysis Data were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median (minimum–maximum), as appropriate. Group comparisons were performed using Student’s t-test or Welch’s t-test according to the homogeneity of variances. Categorical variables, including the presence or absence of the nasal bone and maternal chronic diseases, were compared using Fisher’s exact test. The diagnostic value of clinical measurements to differentiate DS cases from controls was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Optimal cut-off values for NBL, BPD/NBL, and NBL-MoM were determined using Youden’s index. For ROC analyses, fetuses in whom the nasal bone could not be visualized were assigned an NBL value of 0.5 mm, representing the minimal measurable length, to allow inclusion in ratio-based calculations. Additional stratified ROC analyses were conducted in the detectable nasal bone subgroup to avoid potential bias from combining absent and hypoplastic cases. Previously reported cut-offs from the literature were also considered. Diagnostic performance (sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative likelihood ratios with 95% confidence intervals) was calculated for both binary nasal bone presence and the evaluated cut-offs. Additionally, univariate linear regression models were used to analyze the relationship between gestational age and NBL, BPD/NBL, and NBL-MoM. All analyses were conducted using R statistical software (version 4.1.2). The ‘reportROC’ package was used for diagnostic performance evaluation. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Median, 2.5th, 5th, 95th and 97.5th percentile values of nasal bone measurements between 17 and 25 weeks of the control group are presented in Table . Linear regression analyses were used to examine the change in NBL and BPD/NBL ratio according to gestational age (independent variable) in fetuses with a detectable nasal bone (NBL > 0). There was a linear relationship between nasal bone length and gestational week (GW): NBL = 0.38 × (GW) – 1.12 (R² = 0.31; SE = 0.01; p < 0.001) (Fig. ). There was no linear relationship between BPD/NBL and gestational week (GW): BPD/NBL = 0.02 × (GW) + 7.0 (R² = 0.0004; SE = 0.01; p = 0.247) (Fig. ). There was a linear relationship between the length of the nasal bones and biparietal diameter (Fig. ). NBL = 0.101 × (BPD) + 1.83 (R² = 0.275; SE = 0.003; p < 0.001). There was a linear relationship between nasal bone length multiples of the median (NBL-MoM) and gestational week (GW): NBL-MoM = 0.02 × (GW) + 0.38 (R² = 0.082; SE = 0.01; p < 0.001) (Fig. ). Mean age of mothers in the DS group

BPD/NBL and gestational week (GW): BPD/NBL = 0.02 × (GW) + 7.0 (R² = 0.0004; SE = 0.01; p = 0.247) (Fig. ). There was a linear relationship between the length of the nasal bones and biparietal diameter (Fig. ). NBL = 0.101 × (BPD) + 1.83 (R² = 0.275; SE = 0.003; p < 0.001). There was a linear relationship between nasal bone length multiples of the median (NBL-MoM) and gestational week (GW): NBL-MoM = 0.02 × (GW) + 0.38 (R² = 0.082; SE = 0.01; p < 0.001) (Fig. ). Mean age of mothers in the DS group was significantly higher than in the control group ( p < 0.001). There was no significant difference between groups regarding gravidity, parity, pre-pregnancy BMI, maternal chronic disease, gestational week and BPD (Table ). Ethnicity was not systematically recorded in the database. The study population was derived from a single tertiary center serving a predominantly Turkish and Kurdish population. Table shows the comparison between DS and control groups regarding NBL (mm), BPD/NBL ratio and NBL-MoM values among fetuses with a detectable nasal bone. Mean nasal bone length was significantly lower in the DS group ( p < 0.001). Mean BPD/NBL ratio was significantly higher in fetuses with Down syndrome than in the control group ( p < 0.001). NBL-MoM values differed significantly between DS and control groups ( p < 0.001). Table shows the predictive value of nasal bone absence for Down syndrome. Among the 35 fetuses with Down syndrome, 14 (40%) had absent nasal bone, whereas nasal bone was present in 3069 controls ( p < 0.001). Nasal bone absence demonstrated a sensitivity of 40% and a specificity of 100%. Nasal bone absence had a positive likelihood ratio (LR⁺) of 1228, indicating that a fetus without a detectable nasal bone is considerably more likely to have Down syndrome than a fetus with a visible nasal bone. The negative likelihood ratio (LR⁻) was 0.60. The diagnostic accuracy of nasal bone length (NBL) at different cut-off values is presented in Table . An absolute NBL cut-off < 2.5 mm yielded 49% sensitivity and 99.9% specificity. Percentile-based thresholds performed better: the 2.5th percentile provided 86% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity, whereas the 5th percentile increased sensitivity to 94% with a specificity of 96.4%. Figure shows the ROC curve for predicting fetuses with DS using the BPD/NBL ratio. Using a cut-off of 9 or greater identified 93% of DS fetuses and 97.5% of euploid fetuses (LR⁺ = 37). The diagnostic performance across all evaluated BPD/NBL cut-off values is summarized in Table . To evaluate whether the inclusion of absent nasal bone cases biased the ROC analysis, additional stratified ROC analyses were performed in the detectable nasal bone subgroup, with similar diagnostic performance (Supplementary Table ). Analysis of the ROC curve showing the predictive value of NBL-MoM for Down syndrome is presented in Fig. . NBL-MoM thresholds of < 0.65, < 0.75, < 0.76, and < 0.80 were evaluated, and their diagnostic performances are presented in Table . Discussion In our study, we established a nomogram for nasal bone (NBL) measurements between 17 and 25 weeks of gestation in our own population. In addition to the high sensitivity and specificity of absent and hypoplastic nasal bone in predicting Down syndrome (DS), we found that the 5th percentile of NBL, a NBL-MoM value of < 0.65, and a BPD/NBL ratio of 9 were significantly effective in predicting DS within our population. A particular strength of our study is that it enables accurate identification of healthy fetuses in our population with a low false-positive rate, which may help reduce maternal anxiety when used as part of DS screening. A further strength of our study is the comprehensive methodological approach, including the evaluation of absolute measurements, percentile-based thresholds, biometric ratios, and NBL-MoM -based indices within the same cohort, which enhances the robustness and reproducibility of our results. While cfDNA testing stands out as the most sensitive approach for first-trimester aneuploidy screening, its integration into routine practice remains challenging in our country, largely due to economic constraints—a limitation likewise observed in numerous other healthcare systems [ , ]. A further cost-efficient approach entails assessing nuchal translucency (NT) in fetuses with a crown-rump length (CRL) ranging from 45 to 84 mm, serving as a practical first-trimester screening method [ ]. Observing the nasal bone during screening has been shown to enhance the diagnostic performance of the test [ ]. In contrast, when the nasal bone is not visualized, the resulting increase in variability often renders counseling families considerably more difficult. In the first trimester, visualizing the fetal nasal bone often presents considerable challenges. Even under the expertise of seasoned sonographers, more than 71% of cases initially assessed as absent or inconclusive during successive short-interval examinations were later confirmed to have an

a crown-rump length (CRL) ranging from 45 to 84 mm, serving as a practical first-trimester screening method [ ]. Observing the nasal bone during screening has been shown to enhance the diagnostic performance of the test [ ]. In contrast, when the nasal bone is not visualized, the resulting increase in variability often renders counseling families considerably more difficult. In the first trimester, visualizing the fetal nasal bone often presents considerable challenges. Even under the expertise of seasoned sonographers, more than 71% of cases initially assessed as absent or inconclusive during successive short-interval examinations were later confirmed to have an identifiable nasal bone. This finding highlights that the inability to detect the nasal bone in early gestation does not necessarily indicate its true absence [ ]. In contrast, assessment of the nasal bone during the second trimester is generally more feasible and reliable, making it a practical component of mid-trimester screening protocols for Down syndrome [ ]. When an isolated absent or hypoplastic nasal bone is identified in the first trimester, current recommendations favor conducting a detailed follow-up assessment in the second trimester rather than proceeding directly to invasive diagnostic testing [ ]. When screening for trisomy 21, relying solely on maternal age or second-trimester serum biochemistry yields detection rates of approximately 30% and 65%, respectively, each associated with a 5% false-positive rate [ ]. Given the realities in our country, where many pregnant women are unable to attend routine visits during the first trimester, there is a clear need for an effective screening strategy applicable beyond early pregnancy. Consequently, exploring more reliable screening options after 14–15 weeks of gestation represents a reasonable approach. In the second trimester, nasal bone hypoplasia has been shown to identify cases of trisomy 21 more effectively than a simple assessment of nasal bone presence or absence [ ]. Therefore, conducting a comprehensive screening around the 16th week of gestation and beyond—one that includes assessment of absent or hypoplastic nasal bone together with other soft markers—and subsequently referring the patient for invasive testing when indicated may represent a more practical strategy [ ]. Numerous studies have advocated a similar methodological approach [ – ]. Implementing this strategy in low-resource settings is expected to reduce both overall costs and the number of invasive procedures performed. Another study reported that in a population with a high prevalence of first-trimester screening—approximately 90%—the majority underwent either first-trimester combined screening (69%) or cfDNA testing (24%) as their primary screening modality [ ]. In a cohort of pregnancies at or beyond 18 weeks’ gestation with hypoplastic nasal bone (NB) as the primary ultrasound indication, 127 diagnostic amniocenteses were performed. Overall, a major chromosomal abnormality was identified in 22 cases (17%), of which 16 were trisomy 21. Among the 47 cases with hypoplastic NB accompanied by an additional soft marker or structural anomaly (non-isolated hypoplastic NB), chromosomal abnormalities were detected in 14 (30%). Notably, three of these involved pathogenic CNVs that would have been missed by cfDNA screening [ ]. This population-based study, focusing on fetuses undergoing prenatal diagnosis for hypoplastic NB detected in the second trimester, reinforces the strong association between this marker and trisomy 21. It also demonstrates an elevated risk of atypical chromosomal abnormalities when other ultrasound anomalies are present. While no abnormalities other than trisomy 21 were found among our cases of isolated hypoplastic NB, the upper limit of the confidence interval reached 5%. These findings provide valuable data to inform decisions about the need for diagnostic testing following a low-risk cfDNA result [ ]. Bromley et al. [ ] observed the absence of the nasal bone in 6 out of 16 cases of Down syndrome between 15 and 20 weeks’ gestation, whereas this finding was present in only 0.5% of euploid fetuses. Similarly, other retrospective studies have reported an absence of the nasal bone in approximately 40–45% of Down syndrome cases identified during the second and third trimesters [ , ]. A study from China reported an absence of the nasal bone in only 0.13% of euploid fetuses following first-trimester screening, and identified a strong association between this finding and aneuploidy [ ]. Consistent with the existing literature, our study identified absent nasal bone in 40% of Down syndrome cases, while this finding was present in only 0.03% of euploid fetuses—significantly lower than the previously reported rates of 0.5% or 0.13%. This discrepancy may be attributable to the widespread implementation of comprehensive first-trimester screening in our population, as well as the inherently low prevalence of absent nasal bone in our region. These observations represent a noteworthy finding that warrants further investigation. Meta-analyses conducted by Moreno-Cid et al. [ ] and Agathokleous et al. [ ] reported positive likelihood ratios (PLR) ranging from 40.08 to 66.75 and negative likelihood ratios (NLR) of 0.71 for absent nasal bone. In

Down syndrome cases, while this finding was present in only 0.03% of euploid fetuses—significantly lower than the previously reported rates of 0.5% or 0.13%. This discrepancy may be attributable to the widespread implementation of comprehensive first-trimester screening in our population, as well as the inherently low prevalence of absent nasal bone in our region. These observations represent a noteworthy finding that warrants further investigation. Meta-analyses conducted by Moreno-Cid et al. [ ] and Agathokleous et al. [ ] reported positive likelihood ratios (PLR) ranging from 40.08 to 66.75 and negative likelihood ratios (NLR) of 0.71 for absent nasal bone. In contrast, for nasal bone hypoplasia, PLR values ranged between 15.15 and 23.27, with NLR values of 0.46 to 0.47. These findings underscore the ethnic variation and diagnostic heterogeneity present across studies, highlighting the necessity for each population to establish its own reference standards for nasal bone assessment—thereby providing the rationale for conducting our study. Similar population-specific nomograms have also been reported in Turkish cohorts. Yanık et al. [ ] and Göynümer et al. [ ] demonstrated gestational age–specific nasal bone distributions and emphasized the importance of locally derived thresholds. Our findings are consistent with these reports and further support the use of population-based reference standards. To account for gestational age and enhance diagnostic reliability, researchers have adopted various measurement strategies. Notably, definitions of nasal bone hypoplasia differ across the literature: some rely on absolute nasal bone length thresholds (e.g., < 2.5 mm) [ ], while others utilize percentiles [ ], NBL-MoM [ ], or ratios such as BPD/NBL [ ]. This variability underscores the lack of a universal standard and the importance of contextualizing diagnostic criteria. In a prospective study involving 1,046 high-risk pregnancies, nasal bone hypoplasia—defined as either absent or measuring < 2.5 mm—was identified in 61.8% of Down syndrome cases and in only 1.2% of euploid cases. The presence of hypoplasia increased the prior risk nearly 50-fold, whereas the detection of a normal nasal bone reduced the risk by half [ ]. In our study, the mean and median nasal bone lengths in the 21 Down syndrome cases were 4.1 ± 1.18 mm and 4.4 mm (range: 2–6), respectively, compared to 6.76 ± 0.85 mm and 6.7 mm (range: 2–10.7) in the control group, demonstrating a statistically significant difference. Using a threshold of < 2.5 mm yielded a sensitivity of 49% and a specificity of 99.9%. This cut-off increased the risk of Down syndrome by 746-fold, while measurements above this threshold reduced the risk to 0.52 times the baseline. Given the low sensitivity observed in our population, the 2.5 mm cut-off was deemed insufficient. Bunduki et al. [ ] defined nasal bone hypoplasia as a measurement below the 5th percentile and found this in 59.1% of 22 Down syndrome cases, compared to 5.1% among 1,600 euploid fetuses. Shi et al. [ ] employed a < 2.5 percentile threshold using the MCA method and identified chromosomal anomalies in 9% of cases. In another study utilizing the same 2.5 percentile cut-off, 12.7% of fetuses were found to have aneuploidy [ ], while two separate studies from India reported even higher rates of 21% and 26.9%, respectively [ , ]. In our cohort, the 2.5th and 5th percentile thresholds demonstrated sensitivities of 86% and 94% and specificities of 98.9% and 96.4%, respectively, yielding PLRs of 75 and 27, and NLRs of 0.15 and 0.06. The 5th percentile cut-off proved to be more effective for our population. Bromley et al. [ ] recommended using a BPD/NBL ratio greater than 10 for the detection of Down syndrome, noting that this criterion was present in 81% of Down syndrome fetuses compared to 11% of euploid fetuses. In our study, BPD/NBL ratios remained stable throughout gestation. Among Down syndrome cases, the mean and median ratios were 12.83 and 10.77, respectively, whereas these values were 7.3 and 7.25 in the control group. Using cut-off values of 8.5 and 9 yielded sensitivities of 96.6% and 93% and specificities of 93% and 97.5%, respectively, with corresponding PLR and NLR estimates indicating strong diagnostic performance. Odibo et al. [ ] compared various cut-off points, including NBL-MoM thresholds of < 0.75, < 0.5, and < 0.25 as well as a BPD/NBL ratio > 11. While NBL-MoM < 0.75 and BPD/NBL > 11 demonstrated comparable sensitivities (49% and 61%, respectively), NBL-MoM < 0.75 exhibited a significantly higher specificity (92% vs. 84%), making it a more effective parameter. In our cohort, the mean and median NBL-MoM values were 0.50 and 0.54 for Down syndrome cases, compared to 0.82 and 0.81 among controls. Applying cut-offs of < 0.65, < 0.75, and < 0.80 yielded sensitivities of 97%, 98%, and 97%, alongside specificities of 80%, 100%, and 54%, respectively. The < 0.65 threshold demonstrated statistically significant performance, underscoring its diagnostic utility. Importantly, to minimize

BPD/NBL ratio > 11. While NBL-MoM < 0.75 and BPD/NBL > 11 demonstrated comparable sensitivities (49% and 61%, respectively), NBL-MoM < 0.75 exhibited a significantly higher specificity (92% vs. 84%), making it a more effective parameter. In our cohort, the mean and median NBL-MoM values were 0.50 and 0.54 for Down syndrome cases, compared to 0.82 and 0.81 among controls. Applying cut-offs of < 0.65, < 0.75, and < 0.80 yielded sensitivities of 97%, 98%, and 97%, alongside specificities of 80%, 100%, and 54%, respectively. The < 0.65 threshold demonstrated statistically significant performance, underscoring its diagnostic utility. Importantly, to minimize potential bias arising from combining fetuses with absent and hypoplastic nasal bones, we additionally performed stratified analyses restricted to cases with a detectable nasal bone, and similar diagnostic performance was observed. This confirms that the predictive value of hypoplasia is independent of complete nasal bone absence. This retrospective study, conducted over an 11-year period and encompassing 3,070 cases, allowed us to establish gestational age–specific reference standards for nasal bone length in our population. Limitations The retrospective single-center design imposes certain limitations and may restrict generalizability. Because many pregnancies in our setting undergo early first-trimester screening, some affected cases may have been diagnosed and terminated before the second trimester, potentially introducing selection bias. In addition, referrals from other centers may have contributed to cohort heterogeneity. Genetic analyses were not performed in all cases from which nasal bone percentiles were derived, and genetic confirmation was not universally available for fetuses identified with absent or hypoplastic nasal bone. Similarly, euploid status in the control group was inferred from normal postnatal outcomes rather than systematic karyotyping. Although this approach is widely accepted in prenatal screening studies, a small risk of misclassification cannot be entirely excluded. Because ethnicity was not formally recorded, potential ethnic variation in nasal bone measurements could not be directly evaluated. Given that nasal bone measurements may vary across ethnic groups, external validation in diverse populations is warranted. Prospective multicenter studies conducted between 17 and 25 weeks’ gestation are required to externally validate these findings. While it remains premature to define precise detection rates for combined strategies incorporating maternal age, biochemical markers, and ultrasonographic parameters, our results suggest that second-trimester nasal bone assessment may serve as a useful adjunctive marker in Down syndrome risk stratification. Conclusion Considering our findings, assessment of the fetal nasal bone between 17 and 25 weeks of gestation may contribute to mid-trimester risk stratification for Down syndrome. Given the known influence of population-specific variability, locally derived reference ranges may improve screening performance. In our cohort, the 5th percentile NBL threshold, a BPD/NBL ratio ≥ 9, and an NBL-MoM cut-off < 0.65 demonstrated strong discriminatory performance. However, prospective multicenter validation studies are warranted before broad clinical implementation. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1. Supplementary Material 2.

documents.title: SMFM Consult Series 66 Anesthetic Considerations for Pregnant Patients

chunks.content: Introduction The 2025 ESC Guidelines on pregnancy and cardiovascular disease (CVD), endorsed by the European Society of Gynecology (ESG), replace the 2018 edition and integrate the substantial evidence generated over the past seven years, including data from international disease registries. These guidelines are presented as a single, comprehensive document addressing pregnancy across the full spectrum of CVDs, reflecting three key considerations. First, organizational pathways, management models, and therapeutic indications and contraindications are largely shared across different CVDs during pregnancy. Second, maternal cardiovascular risk stratification has evolved and is now anchored to the modified World Health Organization 2.0 (mWHO 2.0) classification, incorporating evidence from the CARPREG II study published in 2018 ( ). Third, despite the heterogeneity of cardiovascular conditions and the need for disease-specific recommendations, optimal care consistently depends on multidisciplinary expertise. This has led to the formalization of expert teams, conceptualized in the new guidelines as the Pregnancy Heart Team (PHT). Accordingly, the guidelines provide both shared recommendations applicable across multiple CVDs and disease-specific guidance aligned with existing ESC documents for individual conditions, including cardiomyopathies, heart failure, arrhythmias, , genetic and non-genetic aortopathies and arteriopathies, pulmonary arterial hypertension, , pulmonary embolism, congenital heart disease, valvular heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, , hypertension, cardio-oncology, and long-term cardiovascular consequences of adverse pregnancy outcomes. Overall, the document introduces 33 new and 10 revised recommendations, some upgraded or downgraded in class or level of evidence. Given the ethical and practical challenges of conducting randomized trials in pregnant populations, only one of the 207 recommendations reaches Class IA, and only 16 are Class IB. The majority are based on expert consensus (Level C evidence), and only nine recommendations are classified as Class III (not recommended) ( ). This review summarizes the main innovations in shared management strategies and disease-specific pathways, while acknowledging that guideline-based recommendations cannot encompass all clinical scenarios. The right to maternity Reproductive choices of women with CVD must be fully respected, provided that decisions are informed and autonomously made. Maternity is a fundamental human right recognized in European law, notably in Article 33 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and reinforced by EU Directive 92/85/EEC, building on the principles of the European Social Charter. These frameworks protect women from discrimination, promote maternal health throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period, and support the reconciliation of family and professional life. Once reproductive decisions are acknowledged as conscious and autonomous, cardiovascular specialists within the PHT have the responsibility to accompany and protect women with CVD throughout their reproductive journey. This includes providing comprehensive and comprehensible information, verifying patient understanding, and delivering individualized, committed care at every stage. While certain severe conditions may contraindicate pregnancy, many women with CVD can achieve successful outcomes with appropriate planning and monitoring. A paradigmatic example is the series by van den Bersselaar et al. , reporting 121 pregnancies in 43 women with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (vEDS) without pregnancy-related deaths, arterial dissections, or uterine ruptures. These data support the upgrade of recommendations regarding pregnancy in vascular EDS from Class IIIC (2018) to Class IC in the new guidelines (Table 5, Section E, ref. 1). Similarly, the persistence of many autosomal dominant CVDs across generations demonstrates that numerous pregnancies in affected women, often unaware of their diagnosis, have been uneventful. Common recommendations for all pregnancies, irrespective of the specific CVD a) The Pregnancy Heart Team (PHT) In the 2025 guidelines, the PHT—anticipated in the 2018 document—assumes a clearly defined and structured role. The PHT is responsible for cardiovascular risk assessment and management using the updated mWHO 2.0 classification, incorporating CARPREG II evidence. Its guiding principle is comprehensive care across the entire reproductive continuum, from preconception counselling to postpartum follow-up, in women with both acquired and genetic CVD. The guidelines introduce two Class I, Level C recommendations mandating PHT involvement for women in mWHO 2.0 high-risk categories (II–III, III, and IV). The guidelines strongly recommend a formal multidisciplinary PHT, including expertise in cardiovascular medicine (medical, interventional, and surgical), obstetrics and gynaecology, anaesthesiology, intensive care, cardiovascular imaging, pharmacology, and genetics). Syndromic or multisystem diseases require additional specialty input, as well as psychological and logistical support ( ). Formal PHT establishment may be challenging in some healthcare settings. In practice, cardiologists often coordinate multidisciplinary pathways even in the absence of an institutionally defined team. This model has been applied for over two decades in our centre for inherited syndromic and non-syndromic cardiovascular diseases, and progressively expanded to disease-tailored multispecialty collaborations ( ). b) Imaging During Pregnancy Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are the safest and preferred imaging modalities during pregnancy. Ultrasound remains first-line for foetal assessment, while MRI is indicated when ultrasound is insufficient or cross-sectional imaging is required. Imaging involving ionizing radiation (X-ray, CT, PET/SPECT) should be avoided whenever possible and reserved for situations in which it is

cardiologists often coordinate multidisciplinary pathways even in the absence of an institutionally defined team. This model has been applied for over two decades in our centre for inherited syndromic and non-syndromic cardiovascular diseases, and progressively expanded to disease-tailored multispecialty collaborations ( ). b) Imaging During Pregnancy Ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are the safest and preferred imaging modalities during pregnancy. Ultrasound remains first-line for foetal assessment, while MRI is indicated when ultrasound is insufficient or cross-sectional imaging is required. Imaging involving ionizing radiation (X-ray, CT, PET/SPECT) should be avoided whenever possible and reserved for situations in which it is clinically indispensable. Guidance from international regulatory bodies confirms that diagnostic radiological procedures are generally safe when medically justified and performed using optimized protocols. These include careful risk–benefit assessment, dose minimization, selective shielding, and thorough patient counselling. The overarching principle is adherence to ALARA (‘As Low As Reasonably Achievable’), ideally maintaining foetal exposure below 50 mGy (Class IC). In life-threatening scenarios, such as suspected aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism, imaging must not be withheld, as timely diagnosis is critical for maternal and foetal survival. c) What Women Should Know About Pregnancy and CVD Structured, multidisciplinary counselling is central to care for all women with CVD considering pregnancy. Counselling should address gynaecological and obstetric history, cardiovascular diagnosis, pharmacological therapy, maternal and foetal risks, and the anticipated intensity of monitoring. Beyond risk communication, counselling must ensure genuine understanding to support autonomous decision-making. These principles are particularly relevant for genetic CVDs, where rapid advances necessitate precise phenotypic and genotypic characterization. d) What Women Should Know About Their Specific CVD The guidelines provide disease-specific recommendations covering cardiomyopathies, heart failure, arrhythmias, prior peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM), aortopathies and arteriopathies, pulmonary hypertension, congenital heart disease, pulmonary embolism, valvular heart disease, coronary artery disease, hypertension, cardio-oncology, heart transplantation, , and long-term cardiovascular risk after pregnancy. Although many recommendations already exist within disease-specific ESC guidelines, their integration into a single document facilitates comparison, harmonization, and clinical implementation. This approach improves understanding of indications and contraindications, timing, and modalities of medical therapy, interventional procedures, and cardiovascular surgery across different disease entities. e) The Genetic Pathway in CVD and Pregnancy <underline>Known genetic disease</underline> Most genetic CVDs are autosomal dominant; when the mother is affected, counselling addresses both maternal and foetal risk. Management includes optimizing maternal safety, potentially through preventive interventions before pregnancy. Autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive conditions primarily raise foetal risk, as parents are usually asymptomatic carriers; females carriers of X-linked recessive defects may develop mild and late phenotypes. Vice versa, in the very rare X-linked dominant disorders, both maternal and reproductive risks are involved. In maternally inherited mitochondrial diseases counselling is complex due to variable phenotype expressivity (heteroplasmy), making both maternal and foetal risks difficult to predict. Reproductive options include prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, with foetal loss rates of 0.1–0.2%) and non-invasive prenatal testing for common aneuploidies (Trisomy 21, 18, 13). Preimplantation Genetic Diagnosis (PGD) is performed during in Vitro Fertilization to screen embryos before transfer. It carries risks related to assisted reproduction (e.g. multiple pregnancies, hormonal treatments); guidelines recommend single-embryo transfer for women with CVD. <underline>Unrecognized genetic disease</underline> Pregnancy can contribute to unmasking an existing genetic CVD that is currently asymptomatic and unrecognized. In such cases, cardiovascular specialists may be the first to suspect a genetic aetiology, often in the context of unexpected complications. This can be particularly difficult to suspect when complications known to be associated with particular genetic diseases occur in women with prior uneventful successful pregnancies, or in women with prior complicated pregnancies whose causes went undetected or under-investigated, and therefore unrecognized. In these cases, essential elements are missing to ensure that the pregnancy path fully aligns with clinical guideline recommendations. When a woman with undiagnosed genetic CVD develops pregnancy complications, management requires urgent PHT involvement (onsite or remote), comprehensive risk assessment, monitoring (ECGs, imaging, biomarkers), medication review, individualized planning, including early delivery if necessary, and referral to tertiary centres when feasible. New disease- and condition-specific recommendations Recommended (class/level of evidence) In cardiomyopathies , vaginal delivery is generally preferred; caesarean section is reserved for obstetric indications, severe heart failure (EF <30% or NYHA III–IV), uncontrolled arrhythmias, severe left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) (≥50 mmHg) in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), or vitamin K antagonist use shortly before or during labour (IC). Counselling is recommended regarding recurrence risk in DCM and EF deterioration during pregnancy (IC), and pre-pregnancy PHT counselling is advised in HCM, symptomatic LV dysfunction (EF <50%), or LVOTO ≥50 mmHg (IC). In PPCM , genetic counselling/testing is advised (IIaC), and HF therapy should continue for ≥12 months after complete LV recovery (IIaC). In cardiogenic shock guidelines recommend inotropes/vasopressors (levosimendan, dobutamine, milrinone) (IC). For heart transplantation , the recommendations include delayed pregnancy post-transplant (IC) and close immunosuppressant monitoring at scheduled intervals (IC). For

Counselling is recommended regarding recurrence risk in DCM and EF deterioration during pregnancy (IC), and pre-pregnancy PHT counselling is advised in HCM, symptomatic LV dysfunction (EF <50%), or LVOTO ≥50 mmHg (IC). In PPCM , genetic counselling/testing is advised (IIaC), and HF therapy should continue for ≥12 months after complete LV recovery (IIaC). In cardiogenic shock guidelines recommend inotropes/vasopressors (levosimendan, dobutamine, milrinone) (IC). For heart transplantation , the recommendations include delayed pregnancy post-transplant (IC) and close immunosuppressant monitoring at scheduled intervals (IC). For primary arrhythmias , beta-blockers (nadolol or propranolol) are recommended for LQTS during pregnancy and lactation (IB), with particular attention to LQT2 in the postpartum period (IB). Flecainide plus beta-blockers is recommended in CPVT with prior cardiac events (IC). In supraventricular arrhythmias, low-molecular-weight heparin is indicated in high-risk AF (IC), and flecainide may be added for rhythm control (IIaC); the use of direct oral anticoagulants is contraindicated in pregnancy. For patients with VT, beta-blockers should be used as first-line therapy. Conversely, the use of amiodarone is not recommended in pregnancy and should be limited to women with refractory or life-threatening arrhythmias. Catheter ablation can be considered during pregnancy in cases of drug-resistant SVT and VT, but the procedure should be performed by experienced operators and in centres equipped with non-fluoroscopic mapping techniques (IIaC). During cardiac arrest, left uterine displacement (IC), supradiaphragmatic i.v. access (IC), and unrestricted drug use (IC) are recommended. Aortopathies , congenital heart diseases, and pulmonary arterial hypertension require specialized pre-pregnancy or pregnancy counselling by a multidisciplinary or PHT team (IC recommendations), especially in high-risk conditions such as Fontan circulation or PAH. For venous thromboembolism , immediate diagnostic evaluation is mandatory (IB). For native valve disease , surgery is recommended when there is high maternal mortality risk and other treatments have failed (IIaC). For prosthetic valves disease structured anticoagulation plans are recommended before or immediately upon pregnancy recognition for women with mechanical heart valves (IC). For coronary artery disease , life-threatening causes must be excluded in pregnant women with chest pain (IC); dual antiplatelet therapy duration follows non-pregnant standards with individualized risk assessment IC), and statin continuation may be considered in established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (IIbC). Hypertension targets BP <140/90 mmHg (IB), with recommended i.v. or oral agents for severe hypertension (IC). Adverse pregnancy outcomes should be documented with long-term cardiovascular risk assessment and counselling (IB). Finally, joint management by the PHT and cardio-oncology team is required for cancer patients receiving cardiotoxic therapy (IC). Not recommended (class IIIC) New guidelines do not recommend myosin inhibitors in HCM, prophylactic temporary pacing during delivery in asymptomatic congenital atrioventricular block, and use of ACE-Is, ARBs, ARNIs, MRAs, ivabradine, or SGLT2 inhibitors during pregnancy due to foetal risk. Considerations beyond guidelines Decision-making beyond recommendations In personalized medicine, Class IIa and IIb recommendations may be difficult to apply, particularly in unplanned pregnancies, emergencies, or settings when the door-to-decision may be very narrow, and PHT may not be readily accessible. Tailoring decisions for individual patients requires knowledge, expertise, and skill, and adherence to recommendations can be conflicting. As emphasized in the Preamble of the document, guidelines do not override individual professional responsibility ; thus, the role and responsibility of the specialist’s personal clinical judgment in each different circumstance is critical. When evidence is insufficient to make recommendations Rare but critical scenarios may require immediate decisions with limited evidence including acute complications such as amniotic fluid embolism, , postpartum haemorrhage and acute obstetric coagulopathy, uterine and arterial rupture in undiagnosed vascular Ehlers Danlos, pneumothorax during pregnancy or labour, ineffective spinal analgesia for caesarean section in women with unknown dural ectasia, e.g. Marfan Syndrome and Loeys-Dietz Syndrome, spontaneous coronary dissections in previously healthy women, intracranial heamorrage. , These clinical scenarios are rare but possible. Door-to-decision can be time-sensitive and may require rapid actions for which it may be necessary to balance the time for urgent multidisciplinary assessment when possible. Additional recommendations from novel ESC guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis Attention to pregnancy was recently given by the new guidelines on myocarditis and pericarditis that incorporate six pregnancy-related recommendations: pre-conception counselling in recurrent pericarditis or myocarditis (class IC); nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during pregnancy, anti-inflammatory therapy during lactation, and corticosteroids during pregnancy and breastfeeding in pericarditis (all class IIaC); colchicine and anakinra (both class IIbC) in pericarditis. Can AI support pregnancy heart teams? AI models are increasingly applied to the analysis of clinical and instrumental data in pregnant women with CVD, with the potential to enhance risk stratification, support imaging interpretation, and refine prognostic assessment of maternal and foetal outcomes. Most existing AI tools operate in isolation, addressing single data sources (e.g. ECG, blood pressure, or foetal monitoring) or narrowly defined clinical scenarios. An illustrative example

myocarditis (class IC); nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs during pregnancy, anti-inflammatory therapy during lactation, and corticosteroids during pregnancy and breastfeeding in pericarditis (all class IIaC); colchicine and anakinra (both class IIbC) in pericarditis. Can AI support pregnancy heart teams? AI models are increasingly applied to the analysis of clinical and instrumental data in pregnant women with CVD, with the potential to enhance risk stratification, support imaging interpretation, and refine prognostic assessment of maternal and foetal outcomes. Most existing AI tools operate in isolation, addressing single data sources (e.g. ECG, blood pressure, or foetal monitoring) or narrowly defined clinical scenarios. An illustrative example in maternal care is the AI-guided screening strategy using a digital stethoscope and 12-lead ECG to detect pregnancy-related left ventricular systolic dysfunction in Nigeria. To date, no unified AI system is capable of dynamically integrating heterogeneous clinical information with modified WHO (mWHO) 2.0 risk classes and translating this knowledge into individualized care pathways. Such a platform should adaptively guide the selection, timing, and frequency of diagnostic investigations throughout pregnancy, while balancing maternal cardiovascular risk, foetal safety, and delivery planning. In addition, an AI-assisted platform could provide real-time decision support by calculating risk according to CARPREG II criteria and assigning mWHO 2.0 risk classes. Current guidelines emphasize that ‘ not every hospital needs to establish a dedicated pregnancy heart team (PHT), but each hospital should establish communication and collaboration with nearby expert teams, optimizing emergency and elective referral pathways within a shared-care model ’. In this context, a unified AI platform capable of integrating multidimensional data, guiding investigations, and supporting remote decision-making could substantially strengthen and extend PHT functionality, particularly in settings lacking dedicated multidisciplinary teams. Conclusions While we are reassured by the support of these new ESC guidelines for all elective situations involving pregnancy in women with known CVD, many questions remain in rare but possible emergencies, in situations lacking strong evidence to support recommendations, and women with previously undiagnosed CVDs. In these contexts, multidisciplinary collaboration, specialist judgment, and emerging technological support remain essential to optimize maternal and foetal outcomes.

documents.title: SMFM Diagnosis and Management of Vasa Previa

chunks.content: Introduction Vasa previa is a rare but potentially life-threatening obstetric condition in which fetal blood vessels traverse the cervical membranes near the internal os (the opening of the cervical canal into the uterine cavity), unprotected by Wharton’s jelly (the protective gelatinous connective tissue surrounding umbilical vessels) or placental tissue. If the condition remains undiagnosed and the cervical membranes rupture, the fetal blood vessels may tear, resulting in rapid exsanguination and death. Perinatal mortality exceeds 50% in undiagnosed cases, decreasing to less than 10% when the condition is identified prenatally; therefore, the antenatal diagnosis of vasa previa is crucial for ensuring the best fetal outcomes [ , ]. Vasa previa has traditionally been classified into two types: type one, which is associated with a velamentous cord insertion, in which umbilical vessels traverse the membranes without protection by Wharton’s jelly, and type two, which is associated with accessory or bilobed placentation. A third variant of vasa previa, type three, was recently proposed, characterized by aberrant fetal vessels traversing the cervical membranes near the internal os despite a normal umbilical cord insertion and the absence of placental abnormalities [ , ]. Although the overall incidence of vasa previa is approximately one in 2,500-6,000 pregnancies [ ], the incidence of type three remains unknown owing to its rarity and diagnostic difficulty. In contrast to vasa previa types one and two, type three lacks consistently identifiable structural abnormalities such as velamentous cord insertion or bilobed placenta. However, its risk profile overlaps with that of classic vasa previa, as assisted reproductive technology (ART) and low-lying placenta have also been reported. Because these risk factors are nonspecific, prenatal suspicion and diagnosis remain challenging [ - ]. Although transvaginal sonography combined with color Doppler imaging remains the most effective screening modality for vasa previa, some type three cases may be overlooked when the placental morphology appears normal, placental position improves, or no risk factors are present [ , ]. We report herein a case of type three vasa previa diagnosed in the late third trimester after the apparent resolution of a previously identified low-lying placenta. This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall associated with vasa previa and the necessity of continued third trimester monitoring with transvaginal color Doppler sonography, even after the placenta migrates to a seemingly normal position. Case presentation A 36-year-old woman (gravida seven, para two: two spontaneous vaginal deliveries, two spontaneous abortions, and two induced abortions) with no notable medical or family history conceived spontaneously and was undergoing routine antenatal care at an obstetric clinic. Fetal growth was appropriate for the assumed gestational age, and all maternal laboratory values were within normal limits. A transvaginal ultrasound performed at the referring clinic at 31 weeks of gestation raised the suspicion of an abnormal placental location. Upon referral to our clinic at 33 weeks of gestation, sonography revealed posterior placental implantation with the placental edge located 11 mm from the internal os, consistent with a diagnosis of low-lying placenta, although no abnormal umbilical cord vessels were observed. Given the prior diagnosis of a low-lying placenta, a targeted transvaginal examination with color Doppler was performed at 35 weeks and two days of gestation as part of the follow-up evaluation. At 35 weeks and two days of gestation, follow-up transvaginal sonography demonstrated the migration of the placental edge to 37 mm from the internal os, indicating a normalization of the placental position. However, color Doppler imaging obtained at the same time revealed a fetal vessel traversing the cervical membranes near the internal os with an arterial blood flow pattern (Figure ). Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis confirmed the presence of a fetal vessel running along the cervical membranes adjacent to the internal os, resulting in a definitive diagnosis of vasa previa (Figure ). The patient was admitted as an inpatient the same day and subsequently underwent a cesarean section at 35 weeks three days of gestation. A male neonate weighing 2,782 g and measuring 48 cm in length was delivered, with Apgar scores of seven at 1 min and 5 min. Umbilical arterial blood gas analysis revealed a pH of 7.33. The patient’s postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged on postoperative day five. The neonate was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit on the day of delivery due to prematurity, received treatment for transient tachypnea and neonatal hypoglycemia, and was discharged at 15 days of age. A macroscopic examination of the placenta revealed no lobulations or parenchymal cord insertions; however, a single umbilical artery traversing approximately 14 cm along the membranes was identified, confirming the diagnosis of type three vasa previa (Figure ). Discussion The present case demonstrates the diagnostic challenges inherent with type three vasa previa, a rare variant that lacks the classical risk factors associated with types one and two. In
