This indicates that when clinical EFW suggests a fetus is not at a weight extreme, this assessment is highly reliable. In routine obstetric practice, where the majority of fetuses fall within the normal weight range, this supports the continued use of clinical EFW as a safe and efficient screening tool. Over the past decades, with the evolution of ultrasound technology and equipment, it has become a cornerstone in many fields of modern medicine, particularly in obstetric practice. Continuous improvements have expanded its applications and enhanced its accuracy. However, superiority of EFW over the clinical EFW is still a debatable question in the literature, while some studies suggested superiority of clinical EFW [ , ], but others indicate an overall superiority of the sonographic method [ , , ]. Nevertheless, both clinical and sonographic methods of EFW demonstrate limited accuracy, influenced by various factors that widen their margin of error. Our study aligns with previous research that reports increased error rates in both sonographic and clinical EFW for extreme fetal weights [ , – ]. Dittkrist et al. reported a mean percent error for sonographic EFW of 0.28% ± 8.45% in the group with a birthweight of 3000–3249 g, 5% ± 11% in the group with a birthweight below 2500 g, and 12% ± 8% in the group with a birthweight of 4250–4500 g [ ]. These findings and ours suggest that physicians tend to estimate the fetal weight closer to the average. However, our results emphasize that although weight extremes increases the error range in both clinical and sonographic EFW, the error increases more in clinical EFW, and strengthens the findings of previous studies suggesting that sonographic estimated fetal weight (EFW) is superior in cases of extreme fetal weight [ ]. As low birthweight is associated with increased morbidity, and early induction of labor is sometimes necessary [ ], errors in EFW in cases of small birthweights have been linked to poorer neonatal outcomes, including higher rates of neonatal resuscitation, lower Apgar scores, and decreased pH values [ ]. As such, the importance of detecting these cases is paramount. Our findings, which strengthen the results of smaller and older studies [ , ], demonstrate improved accuracy and greater sensitivity of sonographic EFW in women with birthweights below 2500 g, highlighting the critical value of performing a sonographic EFW whenever fetal growth restriction is suspected. Consistent with findings from previous studies [ ], our research demonstrates the superior accuracy of sonographic methods in estimating birthweights exceeding 4500 g. This result holds significant clinical implications, as 4500 g is the established threshold for recommending cesarean delivery in cases of maternal diabetes, according to ACOG guidelines [ ], and for the general population, as outlined in Israeli guidelines [ ]. Given the inherent margin of error in fetal weight estimation of approximately 10–15% [ – ], which can translate into discrepancies of several hundred grams in cases of macrosomia, enhancing the accuracy of EFW in the upper weight range is of critical importance. This underscores the clinical relevance of our findings. A previous, smaller study reported the superiority of sonographic EFW in tall women [ ]. However, in our study, which included 908 patients with a height ≥ 172 cm, no difference in accuracy between clinical and sonographic EFW was observed in tall women. Additionally, maternal height was not associated with an increased error range in either sonographic or clinical EFW. Data on the effect of parity on EFW accuracy is limited. Cohen et al. reported a 1.5-fold increased risk of overestimation in clinical EFW among nulliparous women [ ]. Our study provides important information for clinicians regarding the increased risk of error in EFW among nulliparous women using both methods, with a greater extent observed in clinical EFW. A possible explanation might be differences in uterine softness or shape between multiparous and nulliparous women; however, this area requires further research. Although the difference between the two EFW methods was statistically significant across most parameters, the absolute difference was approximately 30 g. Consequently, these results do not imply a definitive superiority of sonographic EFW over clinical methods in this subpopulation. Interestingly, while some studies have reported increased error in EFW among obese women, with a tendency towards overestimation [ – ], others have not found an association between obesity and inaccurate EFW [ ]. Our analysis did not find an increased risk for EFW error among obese patients. Similar to findings in other studies [ , ], this research indicates a greater accuracy of sonographic

Consequently, these results do not imply a definitive superiority of sonographic EFW over clinical methods in this subpopulation. Interestingly, while some studies have reported increased error in EFW among obese women, with a tendency towards overestimation [ – ], others have not found an association between obesity and inaccurate EFW [ ]. Our analysis did not find an increased risk for EFW error among obese patients. Similar to findings in other studies [ , ], this research indicates a greater accuracy of sonographic EFW in terms of percentage errors among these patients. However, it is important to note that there was no significant difference observed in absolute errors. This raises questions about the clinical significance of the reported higher accuracy. EFW is routinely used in everyday obstetric practice, playing a critical role in identifying fetuses that may benefit from more frequent follow-up, such as those with growth restriction. EFW is also a key factor in determining the timing and mode of delivery. Errors in EFW can lead to adverse obstetric outcomes and unnecessary medical interventions [ , , ]. Our study highlights the differences in accuracy between sonographic and clinical EFW in various scenarios, providing important evidence-based information for clinicians. This information can aid in determining which method to use and, more precisely, in identifying cases where sonographic EFW is critical. We provided information on specific factors that increase the error range for each EFW method, which is crucial for clinicians to be aware of and to communicate to patients. This information may also influence clinical routines, such as recommending additional EFW by a senior ultrasound specialist in cases of extreme fetal weights. Our study, conducted on a large cohort, establishes a robust foundation for future follow-up studies. To further enhance its clinical implications, prospective studies are necessary to evaluate whether tailoring the use of different EFW methods based on patient characteristics genuinely improves obstetric outcomes. Additional studies utilizing large datasets are required to assess the potential clinical implications of errors in EFW, particularly at the birthweight extremes, and their impact on clinical outcomes. Moreover, as medicine advances towards a personalized, patient-specific approach, future endeavors may aim to develop a tool capable of adjusting EFW based on specific patient characteristics known to influence error range. Our study has several strengths. Notably, it includes a large cohort size, making it one of the largest studies addressing EFW accuracy to date. It addresses crucial and practical questions that arise in everyday practice. We examined various subgroups with different patient characteristics in a single cohort, enabling more precise and patient-specific conclusions to be drawn. There are several limitations of the current study that should be acknowledged. The first is its retrospective nature. A substantial proportion of patients were excluded due to missing EFW data. Despite statistical significance in several variables.For example, mean neonatal birthweight differed by only 46 g between groups (3400 g vs. 3354 g), maternal age by 0.3 years, and maternal height by 0.6 cm. These minimal differences suggest that exclusions were largely related to data availability rather than systematic differences in maternal or obstetric characteristics. Additionally, we lack information about the level of experience of those performing the weight estimations, which is known to impact accuracy [ ]. However, in our department, residents with comparable durations of experience typically conduct EFW upon patient arrival, which suggests minimal interference with the analysis and conclusions. Clinical and sonographic EFW were often performed by the same examiner, which may introduce some degree of observer dependency between methods. This reflects routine clinical workflow and therefore enhances the external validity of the findings. In cases where EFW was < 10th percentile or > 4000 g, a second ultrasound specialist verified the measurement. Our institutional protocol requires specialist re-evaluation when fetal weight is suspected to be below the 10th percentile or above 4000 g. This may have contributed to the observed superiority of sonographic EFW at weight extremes, as ultrasound estimates in these cases were more likely to undergo additional expert validation. However, it mirrors real-world clinical practice, in which suspected growth abnormalities routinely trigger expert review. Although our study was conducted in a single tertiary referral center, the large and heterogeneous patient population enhances the robustness of the findings. Nevertheless, generalizability may be limited by institutional practices, population characteristics, and documentation protocols. Future multicenter studies, including prospective external validation across different healthcare systems and patient populations, are needed to confirm the reproducibility and clinical applicability of our results. Conclusions In conclusion, sonographic EFW demonstrated superior accuracy primarily in cases of extreme fetal weight. Pregnancy and delivery-related data included the presence of diabetes mellitus, gestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders (chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, and preeclampsia), gestational age at delivery, induction of labor, and mode of delivery (vaginal, operative or cesarean delivery (CD)). Gestational age was based on LMP with confirmation by US. Fetal weight estimation Clinical and sonographic EFW were performed on the same day. The most recent paired assessments obtained within ≤ 14 days prior to delivery were used for analysis. More precise timing within this interval was not available in the electronic medical records. Clinical EFW is based on bimanual abdominal palpation (Leopold maneuver) performed by a trained physician from the Obstetrics and Gynecology department. Ultrasound EFW included the standard fetal biometry measurements of AC, FL, BPD and HC. Calculation by the ultrasound machine is based on Hadlock’s formula [ ]. In our department, all women presenting to the labor ward routinely undergo both clinical and sonographic EFW assessments upon admission, as part of our standardized protocol, and not only when growth abnormality is suspected. If there is a recent both clinical and sonographic EFW assessment within the past 14 days from prior evaluations, we rely on that instead of repeating the assessment. This practice aligns with evidence suggesting scan intervals of less than 14 days are not recommended because of high scan error rates [ , ]. EFW was documented by a range of healthcare providers, including both residents and experienced clinicians. However, the majority of EFW assessments were performed by residents with similar levels of experience, as they are typically assigned to the labor and delivery triage

This practice aligns with evidence suggesting scan intervals of less than 14 days are not recommended because of high scan error rates [ , ]. EFW was documented by a range of healthcare providers, including both residents and experienced clinicians. However, the majority of EFW assessments were performed by residents with similar levels of experience, as they are typically assigned to the labor and delivery triage unit .Clinical and sonographic EFW were typically performed by the same clinician during routine admission to the labor ward and were therefore not blinded, which may represent a potential source of observer bias. Both assessments were conducted consecutively before delivery and prior to knowledge of the actual birth weight, reflecting real-world clinical practice. If the EFW is below the 10th percentile or exceeds 4000 g, a second examiner, who is an ultrasound specialist from the hospital’s ultrasound unit, verifies the EFW. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics of the study cohort were reported using descriptive statistics. Comparison of characteristics between included and excluded patients was performed using Welch’s two-sample t-test for continuous variables and the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. To assess differences in absolute errors and absolute percent errors between Leopold and ultrasound estimates and the actual birth weight, we used the paired t-test.For the proportion of absolute errors ≥ 500 g, absolute percent error > 10%, and absolute percent error > 20%, we used the McNemar test statistics for paired samples. A McNemar’s test was performed to compare the performance of ultrasound and Leopold’s maneuvers in terms of sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) across different subgroups and thresholds. In small subgroups, predictive performance measures (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV) may be limited by sparse or zero cells; therefore, absolute and percent error metrics were considered the primary indicators of EFW accuracy. Predictors of high estimation error (defined as errors exceeding 10% of the actual birth weight) for both clinical and sonographic EFW were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, allowing direct estimation of relative risks (RR). The results are presented in the form of relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI).The predictors included were macrosomia of 4000–4499 ≥ grams), macrosomia of ≥ 4500 g [ ]), low Birth weight (2500 ≤ grams [ ]), obesity (BMI ≥ 30), maternal height ≥ 172 (≥ 90th percentile) and multiparity. Post hoc power analysis revealed that a sample size of 2504 patients would be sufficient to detect a 5% difference between sonographic EFW and Leopold to birth weight, under the assumptions of a type I error (two-sided) of 5% and at least 80% power. P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In small subgroups, predictive performance measures (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV) may be limited by sparse or zero cells; therefore, absolute and percent error metrics were considered the primary indicators of EFW accuracy. All statistical analyses were performed using Python, statmodel library, version 3.9.7 . The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Meir Medical Center (Helsinki approval number 0245-23-MMC, approved on October 6, 2024). The Ethics Committee waived the requirement for informed consent, as the data were retrospective and fully anonymized. Results Among 67, 557 deliveries during the study period, a total of 14,400 women were eligible for the study and included in the data analysis (Fig. ). Baseline maternal characteristics and neonatal birthweights were compared between women included in the study and those excluded due to missing EFW data (Supplementary Table S1). Eligible Patients’ characteristics are summarized in Table . Density of distribution of the sonographic and clinical EFW as compared to actual birth weight is illustrated in Fig. . Sonographic EFW demonstrates less variability (lower standard deviation) and higher accuracy in the estimates compared to the clinical EFW. When comparing the accuracy of sonographic vs. clinical EFW to the actual birth weight in the entire study population, the sonographic EFW group demonstrated a statistically significant lower absolute error of > 500 g, as well as all absolute percent error calculations (Table ). However, despite the statistical significance, the absolute differences in grams between the groups were minimal, amounting to only a few grams, and unlikely to have clinical relevance. Differences in sensitivity, specificity, and PPV were minimal and unlikely to be clinically meaningful; therefore, accuracy was primarily assessed using absolute and percent error metrics. NPV was higher for clinical EFW compared to sonographic EFW (54% vs. 44% respectively, p < 0.001). When examining the impact of maternal BMI on the accuracy of EFW, sonographic EFW had statistically significant lower percent

NPV was higher for clinical EFW compared to sonographic EFW (54% vs. 44% respectively, p < 0.001). When examining the impact of maternal BMI on the accuracy of EFW, sonographic EFW had statistically significant lower percent errors among women with obesity, however again with an absolute difference amounting to only a few grams, and no difference in sensitivity, specificity, or PPV between the two methods was observed (Table S2). No significant difference was found in the accuracy of sonographic versus clinical EFW among women with normal weight (Table S3), nor among tall women (Table S4). In the subgroup of low birthweight infants (≤ 2500 g), sonographic EFW demonstrated greater accuracy than clinical EFW across all parameters, including absolute and percentage errors (Table S5). The mean EFW differed by more than 100 g, with clinical EFW showing a tendency toward overestimation. While sensitivity of sonographic EFW was higher, predictive performance measures should be interpreted with caution due to subgroup size. Differences between clinical and sonographic EFW among women with birthweights of 4000–4499 g were statistically significant. However, the absolute difference in the mean EFW was only 58 g. Predictive performance measures were not emphasized due to sparse cells in this subgroup. (Table S6). Among patients with birthweights of ≥ 4500 gr, sonographic EFW was more accurate in about 100 g, in a statistically significant way when looking on absolute errors, and absolute present error of > 10%. (Table S7). Sonographic EFW was found to be statistically significant more accurate across all evaluated parameters in nulliparous women, however the differences are of few precents only (Table S8). No difference was observed between the accuracy of sonographic and clinical EFW in multiparous women (Table S9). Fetal weight estimations using either Leopold’s maneuvers or ultrasound, displaying absolute percent error, including 95% confidence intervals (± 95% CI), are shown in detail in Fig. . Logistic regression analyses were performed to identify significant predictors of high estimation errors (defined as errors greater than 10% of the actual birth weight) in both clinical and sonographic EFW. Nulliparity, low birthweight and macrosomia ≥ 4500 gr were associated with a higher estimation error in sonographic EFW, with an relative risk (RR) of 1.1 (95% CI1.02-1.19), 1.88 (95% CI 1.6–2.21) and 2.21 (95% CI 1.75–2.79) respectively (Table S10. Supplement Fig. 1). In relation to clinical EFW- nulliparity, low birthweight, macrosomia of 4000–4499 g and of ≥ 4500 were associated with a higher estimation error, with RR of 1.23 (95% CI 1.15–1.32), 2.48 (95% CI 2.2–2.8) ,1.37 (95% CI 1.21–1.54) and 3.42 (95% CI 3.19–3.66) respectively (Table S11, supplement Fig. 2). Factors contributing to increased error estimates were observed in both EFW methods, although they were more pronounced in clinical EFW. This may be partially explained by the more subjective nature of clinical EFW, in contrast to the more objective nature of sonographic EFW. This subjectivity could lead to a greater tendency in clinical EFW to assess weights closer to the normal range. Detailed subgroup analyses are presented in Supplementary Tables S2–S11. Discussion This study aimed to investigate the accuracy of clinical vs. sonographic EFW in the general population and among specific subgroups. Among birthweight extremes of ≤ 2500 gr and ≥ 4500 gr sonographic EFW was found to be statistically and clinically significantly more accurate, as demonstrated through absolute and percent errors, as well as greater sensitivity of the sonographic EFW. Logistic regressions also revealed that birthweight extremes of ≤ 2500 gr and ≥ 4500 gr were associated with a high estimation error (> 10%) in both sonographic and clinical EFW, with a greater extent observed in clinical EFW. Additionally, a birthweight of 4000–4499 g was also associated with high estimation error, but only in clinical EFW. In the general population, as well as among subgroups of obese, nulliparous, multiparous and tall women, statistically significant differences were observed ; however, these largely reflected the large sample size rather than clinically relevant differences, as the absolute effects were small and unlikely to alter clinical management. An important and clinically relevant finding is the consistently higher NPV of clinical EFW across BMI, height, and parity subgroups. This indicates that when clinical EFW suggests a fetus is not at a weight extreme, this assessment is highly reliable. In routine obstetric practice, where the majority of fetuses fall within the normal weight range, this supports the continued use of clinical EFW as a safe and efficient screening tool. Over the

This indicates that when clinical EFW suggests a fetus is not at a weight extreme, this assessment is highly reliable. In routine obstetric practice, where the majority of fetuses fall within the normal weight range, this supports the continued use of clinical EFW as a safe and efficient screening tool. Over the past decades, with the evolution of ultrasound technology and equipment, it has become a cornerstone in many fields of modern medicine, particularly in obstetric practice. Continuous improvements have expanded its applications and enhanced its accuracy. However, superiority of EFW over the clinical EFW is still a debatable question in the literature, while some studies suggested superiority of clinical EFW [ , ], but others indicate an overall superiority of the sonographic method [ , , ]. Nevertheless, both clinical and sonographic methods of EFW demonstrate limited accuracy, influenced by various factors that widen their margin of error. Our study aligns with previous research that reports increased error rates in both sonographic and clinical EFW for extreme fetal weights [ , – ]. Dittkrist et al. reported a mean percent error for sonographic EFW of 0.28% ± 8.45% in the group with a birthweight of 3000–3249 g, 5% ± 11% in the group with a birthweight below 2500 g, and 12% ± 8% in the group with a birthweight of 4250–4500 g [ ]. These findings and ours suggest that physicians tend to estimate the fetal weight closer to the average. However, our results emphasize that although weight extremes increases the error range in both clinical and sonographic EFW, the error increases more in clinical EFW, and strengthens the findings of previous studies suggesting that sonographic estimated fetal weight (EFW) is superior in cases of extreme fetal weight [ ]. As low birthweight is associated with increased morbidity, and early induction of labor is sometimes necessary [ ], errors in EFW in cases of small birthweights have been linked to poorer neonatal outcomes, including higher rates of neonatal resuscitation, lower Apgar scores, and decreased pH values [ ]. As such, the importance of detecting these cases is paramount. Our findings, which strengthen the results of smaller and older studies [ , ], demonstrate improved accuracy and greater sensitivity of sonographic EFW in women with birthweights below 2500 g, highlighting the critical value of performing a sonographic EFW whenever fetal growth restriction is suspected. Consistent with findings from previous studies [ ], our research demonstrates the superior accuracy of sonographic methods in estimating birthweights exceeding 4500 g. This result holds significant clinical implications, as 4500 g is the established threshold for recommending cesarean delivery in cases of maternal diabetes, according to ACOG guidelines [ ], and for the general population, as outlined in Israeli guidelines [ ]. Given the inherent margin of error in fetal weight estimation of approximately 10–15% [ – ], which can translate into discrepancies of several hundred grams in cases of macrosomia, enhancing the accuracy of EFW in the upper weight range is of critical importance. This underscores the clinical relevance of our findings. A previous, smaller study reported the superiority of sonographic EFW in tall women [ ]. However, in our study, which included 908 patients with a height ≥ 172 cm, no difference in accuracy between clinical and sonographic EFW was observed in tall women. Additionally, maternal height was not associated with an increased error range in either sonographic or clinical EFW. Data on the effect of parity on EFW accuracy is limited. Cohen et al. reported a 1.5-fold increased risk of overestimation in clinical EFW among nulliparous women [ ]. Our study provides important information for clinicians regarding the increased risk of error in EFW among nulliparous women using both methods, with a greater extent observed in clinical EFW. A possible explanation might be differences in uterine softness or shape between multiparous and nulliparous women; however, this area requires further research. Although the difference between the two EFW methods was statistically significant across most parameters, the absolute difference was approximately 30 g. Consequently, these results do not imply a definitive superiority of sonographic EFW over clinical methods in this subpopulation. Interestingly, while some studies have reported increased error in EFW among obese women, with a tendency towards overestimation [ – ], others have not found an association between obesity and inaccurate EFW [ ]. Our analysis did not find an increased risk for EFW error among obese patients. Similar to findings in other studies [ , ], this research indicates a greater accuracy of sonographic

the two EFW methods was statistically significant across most parameters, the absolute difference was approximately 30 g. Consequently, these results do not imply a definitive superiority of sonographic EFW over clinical methods in this subpopulation. Interestingly, while some studies have reported increased error in EFW among obese women, with a tendency towards overestimation [ – ], others have not found an association between obesity and inaccurate EFW [ ]. Our analysis did not find an increased risk for EFW error among obese patients. Similar to findings in other studies [ , ], this research indicates a greater accuracy of sonographic EFW in terms of percentage errors among these patients. However, it is important to note that there was no significant difference observed in absolute errors. This raises questions about the clinical significance of the reported higher accuracy. EFW is routinely used in everyday obstetric practice, playing a critical role in identifying fetuses that may benefit from more frequent follow-up, such as those with growth restriction. EFW is also a key factor in determining the timing and mode of delivery. Errors in EFW can lead to adverse obstetric outcomes and unnecessary medical interventions [ , , ]. Our study highlights the differences in accuracy between sonographic and clinical EFW in various scenarios, providing important evidence-based information for clinicians. This information can aid in determining which method to use and, more precisely, in identifying cases where sonographic EFW is critical. We provided information on specific factors that increase the error range for each EFW method, which is crucial for clinicians to be aware of and to communicate to patients. This information may also influence clinical routines, such as recommending additional EFW by a senior ultrasound specialist in cases of extreme fetal weights. Our study, conducted on a large cohort, establishes a robust foundation for future follow-up studies. To further enhance its clinical implications, prospective studies are necessary to evaluate whether tailoring the use of different EFW methods based on patient characteristics genuinely improves obstetric outcomes. Additional studies utilizing large datasets are required to assess the potential clinical implications of errors in EFW, particularly at the birthweight extremes, and their impact on clinical outcomes. Moreover, as medicine advances towards a personalized, patient-specific approach, future endeavors may aim to develop a tool capable of adjusting EFW based on specific patient characteristics known to influence error range. Our study has several strengths. Notably, it includes a large cohort size, making it one of the largest studies addressing EFW accuracy to date. It addresses crucial and practical questions that arise in everyday practice. We examined various subgroups with different patient characteristics in a single cohort, enabling more precise and patient-specific conclusions to be drawn. There are several limitations of the current study that should be acknowledged. The first is its retrospective nature. A substantial proportion of patients were excluded due to missing EFW data. Despite statistical significance in several variables.For example, mean neonatal birthweight differed by only 46 g between groups (3400 g vs. 3354 g), maternal age by 0.3 years, and maternal height by 0.6 cm. These minimal differences suggest that exclusions were largely related to data availability rather than systematic differences in maternal or obstetric characteristics. Additionally, we lack information about the level of experience of those performing the weight estimations, which is known to impact accuracy [ ]. However, in our department, residents with comparable durations of experience typically conduct EFW upon patient arrival, which suggests minimal interference with the analysis and conclusions. Clinical and sonographic EFW were often performed by the same examiner, which may introduce some degree of observer dependency between methods. This reflects routine clinical workflow and therefore enhances the external validity of the findings. In cases where EFW was < 10th percentile or > 4000 g, a second ultrasound specialist verified the measurement. Our institutional protocol requires specialist re-evaluation when fetal weight is suspected to be below the 10th percentile or above 4000 g. This may have contributed to the observed superiority of sonographic EFW at weight extremes, as ultrasound estimates in these cases were more likely to undergo additional expert validation. However, it mirrors real-world clinical practice, in which suspected growth abnormalities routinely trigger expert review. Although our study was conducted in a single tertiary referral center, the large and heterogeneous patient population enhances the robustness of the findings. Nevertheless, generalizability may be limited by institutional practices, population characteristics, and documentation protocols. Future multicenter studies, including prospective external validation across different healthcare systems and patient populations, are needed to confirm the reproducibility and clinical applicability of our results. Conclusions In conclusion, sonographic EFW demonstrated superior accuracy primarily in cases of extreme fetal weight. In most term pregnancies, clinical estimation showed comparable accuracy and a higher negative predictive value for ruling out extreme birthweight. These findings support the continued

chunks.content: OBJECTIVE Twin-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) is a serious complication of monochorionic-diamniotic pregnancies that arises from unequal blood flow between vascular anastomoses within a single shared placenta. The hemodynamic imbalance leads to life-threatening hypervolemia with hypertensive heart failure in the recipient twin and hypovolemia with hypoperfusion in the donor. Studies of amniotic fluid collected at the time of fetal intervention for TTTS can provide insights into fetal health. Although extracellular vesicles (EVs) are abundant in body fluids and reflect the biology of the cell of origin, few studies have examined amniotic fluid EVs to study fetal biology. Our objective was to identify fetal adaptations to cardiovascular stress in TTTS by profiling RNA from amniotic fluid EVs (evRNA) and cell-free RNA (cfRNA). STUDY DESIGN This exploratory study compared a convenience sample of second-trimester amniotic fluid from monochorionic-diamniotic twin pregnancies complicated by TTTS and singleton controls. Fetuses with genetic or structural abnormalities were excluded. Small EVs were enriched by differential centrifugation and analyzed using nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, and Western blot for EV markers. EVs were pre-treated with RNase A to minimize any cfRNA contamination. RNA extracted from EV preparations (evRNA) and amniotic fluid supernatants (cfRNA) was used for RNA sequencing. Differential gene expression (fold change [FC] >1.5, q-value <0.1) and gene set enrichment analyses were performed for TTTS vs. control evRNA and cfRNA datasets. Detailed methods are included in the . RESULTS Amniotic fluid EVs from TTTS recipients (n=10) and singleton controls (n=8; ) were 40-160 nm, exhibited small EV morphology ( ), and expressed canonical small EV markers, including CD9, CD81, and Syntenin-1 ( ). EV and total protein concentrations were reduced in TTTS, which was anticipated secondary to recipient twin pathophysiology of hypervolemia and excessive urine production resulting in polyhydramnios ( - ). No differences in EV counts were observed after normalization to protein concentration ( ). Following the removal of low-quality data, the final analysis included 27 of 31 sequenced ( ). Differences in clinical characteristics for the analyzed groups included younger maternal age and later gestational age for TTTS compared with controls ( ). Overall, 62 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified ( - , ). Seven genes (11%) upregulated in TTTS were identified in both datasets and fell into four main functional categories: chromatin accessibility ( SMARCC1 , TAF15 , NCL ); metabolism ( RAB13, MAP4K4 , TRAK2 ); vesicle trafficking ( RAB13 ); and early neurodevelopment ( SH3PXD2A , SMARCC1 , TAF15, MAP4K4 ). Among the unique DEGs in either dataset were genes involved in metabolism ( NDUFA4L2 ), vesicle trafficking ( KIF1C , UACA ), development ( IGF2 , MTURN , PTPN11 ), cell cycle and cancer progression (e.g., ST5, ZC3H13 , UACA, SPINK1 ). For evRNA DEGs, Reactome and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) gene set enrichment analysis using indicated the downregulation of mitochondrial pathways (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation, TCA cycle, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor [PPAR] signaling), hepatic metabolism (amino acid metabolism, cytochrome P450, propanoate metabolism), and mRNA translation (translation elongation, ribosome; ; ). Indeed, amniotic fluid lactate levels were increased in TTTS, consistent with the downregulation of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and a shift toward anaerobic glycolysis ( ). Upregulated pathways were related to endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and oxidative stress (HSP90 chaperone recycling, Golgi to ER retrograde traffic, oxidative stress), cell signaling (estrogen receptor, MET signaling), and cell cycle (DNA repair pathways, M phase). The cfRNA data showed downregulation of genes involved in the metabolism and transport of lipids (lipoproteins, sphingolipids; ). While the specific pathways were distinct from the evRNA results, similar processes were positively enriched in the two datasets, including cell cycle (prophase, DNA replication) and epigenetic regulation (histone deacetylases [HDACs], DNA methylation). The positive enrichment of genes associated with dilated cardiomyopathy – a clinical feature of TTTS – and the negative enrichment of genes involved in translation and oxidative phosphorylation were only identified in the evRNA analysis ( ). These findings suggest that amniotic fluid evRNA profiling may identify relevant and distinct biologic perturbations in complicated fetal conditions. Collectively, our results reveal substantial alterations in metabolism and cell cycle in TTTS. Our work builds upon prior amniotic fluid omics studies in TTTS. , A more complete understanding of TTTS biology could inform the development of prognostic biomarkers to improve care and counseling for patients undergoing laser surgery. Another clinical implication of this work is the potential to elucidate the contributions of in-utero stress to fetal programming and lifetime disease risk in offspring. Interestingly, TTTS was associated with the enrichment of genes involved in epigenetic modifications, a potential mechanism for fetal programming. Future research enrolling larger cohorts with well-matched controls and postnatal follow up are needed. Whether profiling EVs provides a distinct advantage over unfractionated fluid is not known. biology could inform the development of prognostic biomarkers to improve care and counseling for patients undergoing laser surgery. Another clinical implication of this work is the potential to elucidate the contributions of in-utero stress to fetal programming and lifetime disease risk in offspring. Interestingly, TTTS was associated with the enrichment of genes involved in epigenetic modifications, a potential mechanism for fetal programming. Future research enrolling larger cohorts with well-matched controls and postnatal follow up are needed. Whether profiling EVs provides a distinct advantage over unfractionated fluid is not known. We hypothesize that the enrichment of EVs increases the signal-to-noise ratio, favoring active biological pathways given the production of EVs from living cells and protection of luminal RNA from degradation. Although we aimed to understand the biology of TTTS, an equally important endeavor will be to identify the sources and functions of amniotic fluid EVs given the role of EVs as mediators of cell-cell communication and the potential for changes in amniotic fluid EV composition to influence the risk of pregnancy complications, such as preterm birth. , The therapeutic, regenerative potential of amniotic fluid EVs is another area of active research. Future studies of amniotic fluid EVs will contribute to our understanding of human fetal development and disease, pregnancy complications, and novel applications of EVs in medicine. Our study highlights the feasibility of amniotic fluid evRNA analysis and provides additional support for the analysis of amniotic fluid constituents to gain insights into human fetal conditions that lack experimental models. A strength of our study is the analysis of both evRNA and cfRNA and the use of next-generation sequencing. We acknowledge the limitations of our study, including the small sample size, heterogeneity of TTTS cases, and the use of unmatched singleton controls which limits the interpretation of results. Furthermore, amniotic fluid components represent of mixture of signal from many sources and provide only a snapshot of a dynamic system. Nonetheless, amniotic fluid analyses are an invaluable opportunity to assess human fetal development and disease. CONCLUSION Amniotic fluid evRNA and cfRNA profiling provide unique insights into gene expression changes associated with TTTS recipient physiology, including alterations in metabolism in response to hemodynamic stress. chunks.content: The ALPS (Antenatal Late Preterm Steroids) randomized trial demonstrated that antenatal exposure to betamethasone reduced short-term neonatal respiratory morbidity in children of pregnant individuals at risk for delivery from 34 through 36 weeks of gestation. According to these findings, administration of steroids to women at high probability of late preterm birth is now recommended in the United States. , Since this recommendation, there has been a population-level decrease in assisted ventilation in neonates born in the late preterm period. The available literature suggests that adverse neonatal respiratory outcomes after late preterm birth persist beyond the first year of life and into childhood, potentially manifesting as wheezing or asthma, but information is sparse and mainly retrospective. – Data on the effect of antenatal exposure to corticosteroids on childhood asthma are also limited and mixed, with various studies concluding a benefit to administration, a harm to administration, or no effect. – Furthermore, none of these data focus on steroids administered during the late preterm period. To address this question, we performed a follow-up study of the ALPS trial to evaluate whether antenatal betamethasone exposure affected childhood pulmonary outcomes. We hypothesized that the positive effects of betamethasone on lung function at birth might persist to age 6 in children with an expected late preterm delivery. METHODS This is a prospective follow-up study of children of participants enrolled in the ALPS trial, a multicenter, double-blinded randomized trial designed to assess whether antenatal betamethasone administered from 34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks of gestation improved neonatal respiratory outcomes. Details of the parent study have been described previously. All participants of the parent trial were given the option to consent to future contact, and children of those who consented to future contact were eligible for this follow-up study if they were aged 6 years or older and if enrollment occurred at 1 of 13 clinical centers that participated in the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units (MFMU) Network in the 5-year funding cycle from 2011 to 2016 ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). To compare respiratory morbidity in former late preterm and term birth, a reference cohort of children of women at low risk enrolled at term in a concurrent Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development MFMU trial during the same 5-year funding cycle (2011–2016), STAN (A Randomized Trial of Fetal ECG ST Segment and T Wave Analysis as an Adjunct to Electronic Fetal Heart Monitoring), was also followed up and served as the comparison group for the children whose birthing parents were enrolled in ALPS. The STAN participants who were at more than 36 6/7 weeks of gestation at delivery were randomly selected for enrollment and proportionally matched to ALPS participants by MFMU center, sex assigned at birth, and date of birth. Death of the child and an inability to partake in study procedures were considered exclusions. Center-specific lists of potentially eligible participants were given to trained research staff, who used multiple modalities, including phone, social media, email, or mailed cards, to find participants. A website was created to provide information about the follow-up study to participants of the parent trial, and the web address was included in cards mailed to potential participants. Once located, parents or caregivers who were interested in participating in the follow-up study signed consent and their children provided verbal or signed assent specific to the requirements of the corresponding local IRB. Pulmonary function testing was performed by certified study staff, and the caregiver completed a questionnaire related to respiratory symptoms and medication use. Maternal demographics were collected from the parent trial. In addition, research staff collected information on exposure to secondhand smoke, physician diagnosis of asthma in the child, and hospitalization or emergency room visits for a respiratory illness or prescription for asthma medications in the past 12 months by caregiver report and through hospital discharge summary review. Research staff measured the child’s height and weight in a standardized fashion, and children provided urine samples to detect the presence of cotinine, suggestive of secondhand smoke. A 20-mL midstream urine sample was collected, placed in conical tubes, and centrifuged for 5 minutes at 3,000 to 4,000 RPM to pellet any precipitate. The urine was then transferred to 5-mL aliquots with a sterile pipette. Samples were stored at −80°C until they were shipped to a central laboratory at Boston Children’s Health Physicians, LLP. The central laboratory performed a direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to measure cotinine in the urine. Urine cotinine levels of 1 ng/mL or more were considered suggestive of secondhand smoke exposure. Trained and certified research staff performed pulmonary function testing in accordance with the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society standards using Fleish pneumotachometer–spirometers interfaced with customized software (Pneumotrac). Calibration checks of the pneumotachometer with a 3-L syringe and the spirometer with 1–2 healthy individuals (biological control group) were performed on a regular basis before study visits. Prebronchodilator spirometry testing was attempted for all children enrolled. Postbronchodilator spirometry testing was offered to children without contraindications to albuterol. However, children were no longer asked to use the bronchodilator once the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic began because of safety concerns regarding sharing a multiuse inhaler. Children were instructed to take a deep breath and to exhale as fast, hard, and long as possible (ie, the maneuver). The child was asked to repeat the maneuver up to a maximum of eight attempts or until three acceptable maneuvers were obtained. If none of the maneuvers were usable, the child was asked to return for testing in 6 months. Maneuvers were considered usable if there was at least 1 second of data without coughing or taking a breath. Immediate computerized maneuver and session quality feedback was provided during the testing from the spirometry software. Secondary centralized review of all spirometry sessions was performed by a pulmonologist (R.A.W.) monthly, who then provided feedback to the technicians and rejected sessions that did not provide usable spirometry data. All participants, research staff, and investigators remained blinded to treatment assignment in the parent trial. The primary outcome was a composite for childhood respiratory impairment that included any of the following: 1) abnormal spirometry , defined as prebronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ) below the lower limit of normal, FEV 1 /forced vital capacity (FVC) below the lower limit of normal, or FVC below the lower limit of normal, with lower limit of normal defined as the 5th percentile by the Global Lung Initiative; 2) physician-diagnosed asthma per parent or caregiver report and daily asthma medication; or 3) daily asthma medication use in the past year. The Global Lung Initiative reference equations were used to calculate the lower limits of normal based on age, height, sex assigned at birth, and other/mixed ethnicity. The other/mixed reference equation is a composite that takes the average of four ethnic groups (White, African American, North East Asian, and South East Asian) and was used because there is no biological basis for using race-specific calculations of lung function. , Several prespecified subgroup analyses were performed that compared the strength of association for the primary outcome for those randomized to betamethasone and those randomized to placebo: private insurance, cesarean delivery, and child sex. Secondary outcomes included each subcomponent of the primary outcome and the individual spirometry measures as continuous outcomes. The z scores were obtained for the prebronchodilator FEV 1 , FEV 1 /FVC, and FVC with the Global Lung Initiative other/mixed reference equation. The FEV 1 percent change in predicted or percent reversibility was also calculated for those with postbronchodilator spirometry. Questions related to asthma and other respiratory symptoms were assessed with the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood questionnaire, a standardized tool to measure the presence and severity of asthma symptoms. Ever having had pneumonia, wheezing or whistling in the chest, or other respiratory symptoms (coughing, wheezing or shortness of breath) in the past year were also evaluated by caregiver report and through hospital discharge summary review. All outcomes were assessed by parent–trial treatment assignment. In addition, outcomes for the children in ALPS assigned to betamethasone or placebo, all of whom were born to individuals at risk of late preterm birth, were compared with outcomes for children born from the STAN trial, all of whom were born to individuals enrolled at term. Baseline characteristics were compared between individuals who were and those who were not enrolled in the follow-up study and by parent treatment assignment among those enrolled in the follow-up study (betamethasone, placebo, and STAN). Continuous variables were compared with the t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test; categorical variables were compared with the χ test. Log-binomial regression was used to estimate relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs for categorical outcomes, and mixed linear models were used to estimate mean differences and 95% CIs for continuous outcomes. Separate models with interaction terms for treatment assignment and each subgroup (private insurance, cesarean delivery, and sex) were tested for the primary outcome. Analyses

Log-binomial regression was used to estimate relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs for categorical outcomes, and mixed linear models were used to estimate mean differences and 95% CIs for continuous outcomes. Separate models with interaction terms for treatment assignment and each subgroup (private insurance, cesarean delivery, and sex) were tested for the primary outcome. Analyses were adjusted for prespecified characteristics, including maternal education, age at delivery, smoking during pregnancy, asthma requiring medication during pregnancy, and gestational age at delivery, as well as child age at the study visit, body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared), sex, secondhand smoke exposure, and enrollment center. Analyses comparing ALPS children with STAN children did not adjust for maternal asthma requiring medication because this information was not collected in the STAN trial. Gestational age at delivery was also not adjusted for in the STAN analysis because the comparison was late-preterm and term children. Any additional characteristics that differed by group (betamethasone, placebo, and STAN) were also adjusted for in analyses. A child was considered to have secondhand smoke exposure if the primary caregiver or another household member smoked. Cotinine from the child’s urine was used to examine reliability of parent reported secondhand smoke exposure. Values of 50 ng/mL or higher were excluded because they are not within the range expected for children. Cotinine present in urine is suggestive of exposure within the prior 7–10 days. Lost to follow-up was defined as children who consented for the study and either declined spirometry or had invalid spirometry and did not meet the primary outcome based on doctor diagnosis of asthma or medication use. Several sensitivity analyses were performed among ALPS participants. The first included participants lost to follow-up with different assumptions regarding the primary outcome (ie, all had the primary outcome or all did not have the primary outcome). The second sensitivity analysis analyzed only children who had postbronchodilator spirometry measurements to determine whether using these measurements changed the results of the primary outcome. The third sensitivity analysis was conducted among children with urine cotinine measurements to determine whether adjusting for secondhand smoke exposure based on cotinine levels instead of parent-reported secondhand smoke changed the effect of betamethasone on the primary outcome. To adjust for differences in the original ALPS trial population and the participants in the current study, the last sensitivity analysis used inverse probability weighting to approximate the full ALPS cohort. Logistic regression was used to calculate the probability of enrollment in the follow-up study for characteristics that significantly differed by inclusion in the study. Only characteristics that were not missing in the full cohort were used to calculate the weights. The probability of enrollment was then used to calculate inverse probability weights, and the analyses for the ALPS cohort were rerun using the weighted cohort. Bootstrapping was used to construct 95% CIs for RRs and mean differences. P <.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance, and adjustment for multiple comparisons was not conducted. All analyses used SAS 9.4 software. The sample size was fixed by the number of participants in the ALPS clinical trial, which was 2,831 birthing parents and their children. After excluding those who did not consent to future contact, had died, or were enrolled at sites no longer participating in the MFMU Network and assuming an enrollment rate of 82%, we estimated the sample size for this study to be 2,000 ( ). From information in the literature, it was estimated that the primary outcome rate in the placebo group would be approximately 16%. , An overall sample size of 2,000 was deemed sufficient to detect a 30% decrease in the primary outcome rate in the betamethasone group with a power of 85% and 2-sided α of 0.05 or a 30% increase with approximately 80% power. A noninferiority analysis was initially planned to determine whether children in the betamethasone group had lung function similar to a term cohort (STAN). Assuming a sample size of 1,000 children in the betamethasone group, 500 in the STAN (control) group, a primary outcome rate of 10% in the STAN group, and a noninferiority margin of 4%, the planned sample size would provide approximately 80% power to discern that the betamethasone group is not inferior to the STAN (control) group. Betamethasone would be determined to be noninferior if the lower 95% confidence limit for the risk difference was −4 percentage points or greater (ie, closer to zero). RESULTS There were 2,831 birthing parents and children enrolled in the ALPS trial. Of 2,422 potentially eligible participants, 1,204 were excluded from the follow-up study, mostly because of declined participation or an inability to contact ( ). Similarly, of the 1,313 potentially eligible STAN participants, 877 were excluded from this follow-up study, mostly because of declined participation or an inability to contact. Thus, 1,218 ALPS participants and 436 STAN participants were enrolled in the follow-up study between October 2017 and August 2022. Of the 1,218 ALPS participants enrolled, 614 (50.4%) were exposed to betamethasone and 604 (49.6%) to placebo. Children of ALPS participants compared with ALPS nonparticipants in the follow-up study were older and had parents who were less likely to smoke during pregnancy and more likely to have private insurance and a college degree ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Of those in the follow-up study, maternal and neonatal characteristics were similar between those who received betamethasone and those who received placebo ( ). In addition, the follow-up cohort had a similar decrease in neonatal respiratory disease when exposed to betamethasone compared with placebo ( ). Of the 1,218 ALPS participants enrolled, 1,194 successfully completed spirometry (98.0%). There were no differences in the proportions meeting the primary composite outcome of childhood respiratory impairment (35.3% in the betamethasone group and 35.8% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 1.02, 95% CI, 0.87–1.18) or the individual components of the primary outcome ( ). Interaction terms of treatment assignment with private insurance, cesarean delivery, or sex were not significant. Children who had been exposed to betamethasone were less likely to have ever had wheezing or whistling in the chest (40.7% vs 45.5% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 0.88, 95% CI, 0.77–0.996, P =.04), although there were no differences in other evaluated outcomes ( ). Results for the association between betamethasone exposure and the primary outcome did not change in sensitivity analyses that used varied outcome assumptions for participants lost to follow-up or when the analysis was limited to children with postbronchodilator measurements ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Of those enrolled in the follow-up study, 771 ALPS participants (63.3%) and 251 STAN participants (57.6%) provided urine for cotinine immunoassay. Of the 973 valid samples, 210 ALPS participants (28.6%) and 81 STAN participants (33.9%) had urine cotinine levels suggestive of exposure to secondhand smoke. The reliability of parent-reported smoking in the household was low compared with urine cotinine levels (Cronbach α=0.60). Of the 291 participants with evidence of secondhand smoke exposure, 59.5% did not report smoking in the household. Results for the primary outcome did not change when the cohort was limited to children with urine cotinine measurements ( , http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). The sensitivity analysis that used inverse probability weighting to adjust for differences in maternal age, private insurance, and smoking status during pregnancy did not alter the estimates, and none of the primary or secondary outcomes changed significance. The primary outcome remained similar between the groups (36.0% in the betamethasone group and 36.7% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 1.01, 95% CI, 0.85–1.16). In addition, children who had been exposed to betamethasone were less likely to have ever had wheezing or whistling in the chest (41.2% compared with 45.7% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 0.88, 95% CI, 0.77–0.997) ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Childhood respiratory outcomes among children of ALPS participants were also compared with those of children of STAN participants. The STAN children in the follow-up study compared with the ALPS children in the follow-up study were older at follow-up, had been born at later gestational ages, were less likely to have had small-for-gestational-age birth weights, and had higher BMIs; their parents were less likely to have had a cesarean delivery. In addition, parents of STAN children were younger, less likely to have a college degree, and more likely to have private insurance or to identify as Black compared with parents of ALPS children exposed to betamethasone ( ). Of the 436 STAN participants enrolled, 432 successfully completed spirometry (99.1%). Given that the betamethasone group did not differ from the placebo group on the primary outcome, a noninferiority analysis comparing the betamethasone group with the term STAN cohort was no longer the ideal statistical analysis to perform. Of the 436 STAN participants enrolled, 432 successfully completed spirometry (99.1%). Given that the betamethasone group did not differ from the placebo group on the primary outcome, a noninferiority analysis comparing the betamethasone group with the term STAN cohort was no longer the ideal statistical analysis to perform. Comparisons were first made with children born to ALPS participants who had been randomized to the betamethasone group. The proportions meeting the primary composite outcome were 30.8% in the STAN group and 35.3% in the betamethasone group (adjusted RR 1.13, 95% CI, 0.94–1.36). The individual components of the primary outcome were not different by group ( ). The percent change in predicted FEV 1 was significantly lower among those in the betamethasone group (–0.4±14.3 in the betamethasone group and 1.9±9.9 in the STAN group, adjusted mean difference −2.69, 95% CI, −5.37 to −0.01). Wheezing during or after exercise in the past year was also significantly more likely in the betamethasone group (7.2% in the betamethasone group and 4.4% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.77, 95% CI, 1.03–3.06). Because a noninferiority analysis was initially planned, the adjusted risk difference of −3.6% (95% CI, −9.6 to 2.5%) for the primary outcome was also calculated, indicating that the betamethasone group is inferior to the STAN term cohort as anticipated given the lack of treatment difference between the betamethasone and placebo groups. Children of ALPS participants in the placebo group were also compared with children of STAN participants. Similar to the results from the comparison with the betamethasone group, there were no differences in the proportions meeting the primary composite outcome of childhood respiratory impairment (35.8% in the placebo group and 30.8% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.12, 95% CI, 0.94–1.33) or the individual components of the primary outcome ( , available online at http://links.lww . com/AOG/E468). Ever having wheezing or whistling in the chest (45.5% in the placebo group and 36.7% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.21, 95% CI, 1.03–1. 41) and wheezing during or after exercise in the past year were significantly higher in the placebo group (8. 8% in the placebo group and 4.4% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 2.09, 95% CI, 1.25–3.48). The individual components of abnormal spirometry are summarized by group in . DISCUSSION We found that late preterm antenatal corticosteroid exposure in pregnant individuals at risk of preterm birth did not influence the majority of childhood respiratory outcomes but did lower the frequency of ever having wheezing or whistling in the chest in their children aged 6 years or older. These data provide some insight into the trajectory of pulmonary maturation after late preterm birth and are the only data available on pulmonary outcomes after random allocation to betamethasone or placebo in the late preterm period. We also have found that, regardless of betamethasone exposure, children born to individuals at risk of late preterm birth have a greater risk of wheezing during or after exercise in the past year compared with those born at term in the STAN reference cohort. It is known that late preterm offspring have poorer respiratory outcomes compared with term offspring. , Todisco et al compared children born from 34 to 36 weeks of gestation without respiratory complications at birth with their term siblings by performing pulmonary function testing at a mean age of 11.6 years. They found that the preterm-born children had significantly increased residual volume and residual volume to total lung capacity compared with their term siblings. Similarly, Boyle et al found that children who had been born in the late preterm period had a higher risk of asthma and wheezing compared with their term counterparts. No studies have evaluated whether late preterm administration of betamethasone may improve long-term respiratory outcomes, and the available literature on earlier preterm betamethasone and long-term respiratory outcomes is mixed. An epidemiologic study of administrative data by Pole et al found an increased risk of asthma in children of pregnant individuals exposed to antenatal corticosteroids. The authors did not comment on the gestational age of exposure to steroids. Hung and colleagues sought to assess whether the frequencies of asthma and pulmonary dysfunction in children who were born preterm before 32 weeks of gestation with birth weights less than 1,500 g and who did not have neonatal bronchopulmonary dysplasia were related to antenatal corticosteroid exposure. After adjusting for confounders, including gestational age at delivery, they demonstrated a decrease in the rate of asthma after antenatal corticosteroid exposure (odds ratio 0.27, 95% CI, 0.08–0.88). Finally, follow-up of children whose birthing

of pregnant individuals exposed to antenatal corticosteroids. The authors did not comment on the gestational age of exposure to steroids. Hung and colleagues sought to assess whether the frequencies of asthma and pulmonary dysfunction in children who were born preterm before 32 weeks of gestation with birth weights less than 1,500 g and who did not have neonatal bronchopulmonary dysplasia were related to antenatal corticosteroid exposure. After adjusting for confounders, including gestational age at delivery, they demonstrated a decrease in the rate of asthma after antenatal corticosteroid exposure (odds ratio 0.27, 95% CI, 0.08–0.88). Finally, follow-up of children whose birthing parents had been enrolled in the term steroids ASTECS (Antenatal Steroids for Term Elective Caesarean Section) trial did not find a difference in rates of childhood asthma between exposure groups. Our findings are similar to the findings in the ASTECS follow-up. Furthermore, by comparing children from the ALPS trial, 84.3% of whom were born late preterm, with children from the STAN trial, all of whom were born at term, we have shown that wheezing during or after exercise in the past year was more common in the ALPS group. There are a few notable limitations of our findings. We enrolled just more than half of the intended sample size of 2,000 participants, likely because of both the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and the difficulty finding parent trial participants. There is also the possibility of self-selection bias because those who participated in the follow-up study significantly differed from those who did not. However, results of the sensitivity analysis using inverse probability weighting to approximate the full ALPS cohort demonstrated similar results. Secondary outcomes may have also been affected by recall bias because they were reported by the caregiver. We initially estimated a primary outcome rate of 16.0%. With an increased primary outcome rate of 35.0% in the placebo group, our final sample size gave us more than 90.0% power to show either a 30.0% relative decrease (35.0–24.5%) or 30.0% relative increase (35.0–45.5%) in the primary outcome. The initial protocol included postspirometry bronchodilation with albuterol, but this procedure had to be abandoned during the pandemic because of the multiple-use vials and concern for spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). However, examining the data of the participants enrolled before the pandemic who provided postspirometry data did not change our results. Lastly, secondary outcomes were exploratory and thus may have been underpowered. In addition, because there was no adjustment for multiple comparisons, several secondary findings are possibly attributable to chance. The study also has several strengths. It is the only follow-up study of respiratory outcomes after late preterm administration of betamethasone compared with placebo, and it is one of the largest follow-up studies of single-course corticosteroids at any gestational age. Spirometry was performed with central oversight by trained research personnel, and almost all tests provided usable results. The use of a term-born reference cohort allowed us to compare outcomes with those born at term who were not at risk of late preterm birth. Research staff, participants, and investigators remained blinded to treatment assignment, minimizing bias in outcome assessment. In conclusion, administration of late preterm antenatal corticosteroids improved short-term respiratory outcomes but did not affect childhood pulmonary outcomes, aside from ever having less wheezing or whistling in the chest, compared with those exposed to placebo. documents.title: SMFM Consult Series 60 Management of Pregnancies with COVID-19

chunks.content: The ALPS (Antenatal Late Preterm Steroids) randomized trial demonstrated that antenatal exposure to betamethasone reduced short-term neonatal respiratory morbidity in children of pregnant individuals at risk for delivery from 34 through 36 weeks of gestation. According to these findings, administration of steroids to women at high probability of late preterm birth is now recommended in the United States. , Since this recommendation, there has been a population-level decrease in assisted ventilation in neonates born in the late preterm period. The available literature suggests that adverse neonatal respiratory outcomes after late preterm birth persist beyond the first year of life and into childhood, potentially manifesting as wheezing or asthma, but information is sparse and mainly retrospective. – Data on the effect of antenatal exposure to corticosteroids on childhood asthma are also limited and mixed, with various studies concluding a benefit to administration, a harm to administration, or no effect. – Furthermore, none of these data focus on steroids administered during the late preterm period. To address this question, we performed a follow-up study of the ALPS trial to evaluate whether antenatal betamethasone exposure affected childhood pulmonary outcomes. We hypothesized that the positive effects of betamethasone on lung function at birth might persist to age 6 in children with an expected late preterm delivery. METHODS This is a prospective follow-up study of children of participants enrolled in the ALPS trial, a multicenter, double-blinded randomized trial designed to assess whether antenatal betamethasone administered from 34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks of gestation improved neonatal respiratory outcomes. Details of the parent study have been described previously. All participants of the parent trial were given the option to consent to future contact, and children of those who consented to future contact were eligible for this follow-up study if they were aged 6 years or older and if enrollment occurred at 1 of 13 clinical centers that participated in the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units (MFMU) Network in the 5-year funding cycle from 2011 to 2016 ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). To compare respiratory morbidity in former late preterm and term birth, a reference cohort of children of women at low risk enrolled at term in a concurrent Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development MFMU trial during the same 5-year funding cycle (2011–2016), STAN (A Randomized Trial of Fetal ECG ST Segment and T Wave Analysis as an Adjunct to Electronic Fetal Heart Monitoring), was also followed up and served as the comparison group for the children whose birthing parents were enrolled in ALPS. The STAN participants who were at more than 36 6/7 weeks of gestation at delivery were randomly selected for enrollment and proportionally matched to ALPS participants by MFMU center, sex assigned at birth, and date of birth. Death of the child and an inability to partake in study procedures were considered exclusions. Center-specific lists of potentially eligible participants were given to trained research staff, who used multiple modalities, including phone, social media, email, or mailed cards, to find participants. A website was created to provide information about the follow-up study to participants of the parent trial, and the web address was included in cards mailed to potential participants. Once located, parents or caregivers who were interested in participating in the follow-up study signed consent and their children provided verbal or signed assent specific to the requirements of the corresponding local IRB. Pulmonary function testing was performed by certified study staff, and the caregiver completed a questionnaire related to respiratory symptoms and medication use. Maternal demographics were collected from the parent trial. In addition, research staff collected information on exposure to secondhand smoke, physician diagnosis of asthma in the child, and hospitalization or emergency room visits for a respiratory illness or prescription for asthma medications in the past 12 months by caregiver report and through hospital discharge summary review. Research staff measured the child’s height and weight in a standardized fashion, and children provided urine samples to detect the presence of cotinine, suggestive of secondhand smoke. A 20-mL midstream urine sample was collected, placed in conical tubes, and centrifuged for 5 minutes at 3,000 to 4,000 RPM to pellet any precipitate. The urine was then transferred to 5-mL aliquots with a sterile pipette. Samples were stored at −80°C until they were shipped to a central laboratory at Boston Children’s Health Physicians, LLP. The central laboratory performed a direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to measure cotinine in the urine. Urine cotinine levels of 1 ng/mL or more were considered suggestive of secondhand smoke exposure. Trained and certified research staff performed pulmonary function testing in accordance with the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society standards using Fleish pneumotachometer–spirometers interfaced with customized software (Pneumotrac). Calibration checks of the pneumotachometer
