The central laboratory performed a direct enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to measure cotinine in the urine. Urine cotinine levels of 1 ng/mL or more were considered suggestive of secondhand smoke exposure. Trained and certified research staff performed pulmonary function testing in accordance with the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society standards using Fleish pneumotachometer–spirometers interfaced with customized software (Pneumotrac). Calibration checks of the pneumotachometer with a 3-L syringe and the spirometer with 1–2 healthy individuals (biological control group) were performed on a regular basis before study visits. Prebronchodilator spirometry testing was attempted for all children enrolled. Postbronchodilator spirometry testing was offered to children without contraindications to albuterol. However, children were no longer asked to use the bronchodilator once the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic began because of safety concerns regarding sharing a multiuse inhaler. Children were instructed to take a deep breath and to exhale as fast, hard, and long as possible (ie, the maneuver). The child was asked to repeat the maneuver up to a maximum of eight attempts or until three acceptable maneuvers were obtained. If none of the maneuvers were usable, the child was asked to return for testing in 6 months. Maneuvers were considered usable if there was at least 1 second of data without coughing or taking a breath. Immediate computerized maneuver and session quality feedback was provided during the testing from the spirometry software. Secondary centralized review of all spirometry sessions was performed by a pulmonologist (R.A.W.) monthly, who then provided feedback to the technicians and rejected sessions that did not provide usable spirometry data. All participants, research staff, and investigators remained blinded to treatment assignment in the parent trial. The primary outcome was a composite for childhood respiratory impairment that included any of the following: 1) abnormal spirometry , defined as prebronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ) below the lower limit of normal, FEV 1 /forced vital capacity (FVC) below the lower limit of normal, or FVC below the lower limit of normal, with lower limit of normal defined as the 5th percentile by the Global Lung Initiative; 2) physician-diagnosed asthma per parent or caregiver report and daily asthma medication; or 3) daily asthma medication use in the past year. The Global Lung Initiative reference equations were used to calculate the lower limits of normal based on age, height, sex assigned at birth, and other/mixed ethnicity. The other/mixed reference equation is a composite that takes the average of four ethnic groups (White, African American, North East Asian, and South East Asian) and was used because there is no biological basis for using race-specific calculations of lung function. , Several prespecified subgroup analyses were performed that compared the strength of association for the primary outcome for those randomized to betamethasone and those randomized to placebo: private insurance, cesarean delivery, and child sex. Secondary outcomes included each subcomponent of the primary outcome and the individual spirometry measures as continuous outcomes. The z scores were obtained for the prebronchodilator FEV 1 , FEV 1 /FVC, and FVC with the Global Lung Initiative other/mixed reference equation. The FEV 1 percent change in predicted or percent reversibility was also calculated for those with postbronchodilator spirometry. Questions related to asthma and other respiratory symptoms were assessed with the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood questionnaire, a standardized tool to measure the presence and severity of asthma symptoms. Ever having had pneumonia, wheezing or whistling in the chest, or other respiratory symptoms (coughing, wheezing or shortness of breath) in the past year were also evaluated by caregiver report and through hospital discharge summary review. All outcomes were assessed by parent–trial treatment assignment. In addition, outcomes for the children in ALPS assigned to betamethasone or placebo, all of whom were born to individuals at risk of late preterm birth, were compared with outcomes for children born from the STAN trial, all of whom were born to individuals enrolled at term. Baseline characteristics were compared between individuals who were and those who were not enrolled in the follow-up study and by parent treatment assignment among those enrolled in the follow-up study (betamethasone, placebo, and STAN). Continuous variables were compared with the t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test; categorical variables were compared with the χ test. Log-binomial regression was used to estimate relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs for categorical outcomes, and mixed linear models were used to estimate mean differences and 95% CIs for continuous outcomes. Separate models with interaction terms for treatment assignment and each subgroup (private insurance, cesarean delivery, and sex) were tested for the primary outcome. Analyses

those who were not enrolled in the follow-up study and by parent treatment assignment among those enrolled in the follow-up study (betamethasone, placebo, and STAN). Continuous variables were compared with the t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test; categorical variables were compared with the χ test. Log-binomial regression was used to estimate relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs for categorical outcomes, and mixed linear models were used to estimate mean differences and 95% CIs for continuous outcomes. Separate models with interaction terms for treatment assignment and each subgroup (private insurance, cesarean delivery, and sex) were tested for the primary outcome. Analyses were adjusted for prespecified characteristics, including maternal education, age at delivery, smoking during pregnancy, asthma requiring medication during pregnancy, and gestational age at delivery, as well as child age at the study visit, body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared), sex, secondhand smoke exposure, and enrollment center. Analyses comparing ALPS children with STAN children did not adjust for maternal asthma requiring medication because this information was not collected in the STAN trial. Gestational age at delivery was also not adjusted for in the STAN analysis because the comparison was late-preterm and term children. Any additional characteristics that differed by group (betamethasone, placebo, and STAN) were also adjusted for in analyses. A child was considered to have secondhand smoke exposure if the primary caregiver or another household member smoked. Cotinine from the child’s urine was used to examine reliability of parent reported secondhand smoke exposure. Values of 50 ng/mL or higher were excluded because they are not within the range expected for children. Cotinine present in urine is suggestive of exposure within the prior 7–10 days. Lost to follow-up was defined as children who consented for the study and either declined spirometry or had invalid spirometry and did not meet the primary outcome based on doctor diagnosis of asthma or medication use. Several sensitivity analyses were performed among ALPS participants. The first included participants lost to follow-up with different assumptions regarding the primary outcome (ie, all had the primary outcome or all did not have the primary outcome). The second sensitivity analysis analyzed only children who had postbronchodilator spirometry measurements to determine whether using these measurements changed the results of the primary outcome. The third sensitivity analysis was conducted among children with urine cotinine measurements to determine whether adjusting for secondhand smoke exposure based on cotinine levels instead of parent-reported secondhand smoke changed the effect of betamethasone on the primary outcome. To adjust for differences in the original ALPS trial population and the participants in the current study, the last sensitivity analysis used inverse probability weighting to approximate the full ALPS cohort. Logistic regression was used to calculate the probability of enrollment in the follow-up study for characteristics that significantly differed by inclusion in the study. Only characteristics that were not missing in the full cohort were used to calculate the weights. The probability of enrollment was then used to calculate inverse probability weights, and the analyses for the ALPS cohort were rerun using the weighted cohort. Bootstrapping was used to construct 95% CIs for RRs and mean differences. P <.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance, and adjustment for multiple comparisons was not conducted. All analyses used SAS 9.4 software. The sample size was fixed by the number of participants in the ALPS clinical trial, which was 2,831 birthing parents and their children. After excluding those who did not consent to future contact, had died, or were enrolled at sites no longer participating in the MFMU Network and assuming an enrollment rate of 82%, we estimated the sample size for this study to be 2,000 ( ). From information in the literature, it was estimated that the primary outcome rate in the placebo group would be approximately 16%. , An overall sample size of 2,000 was deemed sufficient to detect a 30% decrease in the primary outcome rate in the betamethasone group with a power of 85% and 2-sided α of 0.05 or a 30% increase with approximately 80% power. A noninferiority analysis was initially planned to determine whether children in the betamethasone group had lung function similar to a term cohort (STAN). Assuming a sample size of 1,000 children in the betamethasone group, 500 in the STAN (control) group, a primary outcome rate of 10% in the STAN group, and a noninferiority margin of 4%, the planned sample size would provide approximately 80% power to discern that the betamethasone group is not inferior to the STAN (control) group. Betamethasone would be determined to be noninferior if the lower 95% confidence limit for the risk difference was −4 percentage points or greater (ie, closer to zero). Betamethasone would be determined to be noninferior if the lower 95% confidence limit for the risk difference was −4 percentage points or greater (ie, closer to zero). RESULTS There were 2,831 birthing parents and children enrolled in the ALPS trial. Of 2,422 potentially eligible participants, 1,204 were excluded from the follow-up study, mostly because of declined participation or an inability to contact ( ). Similarly, of the 1,313 potentially eligible STAN participants, 877 were excluded from this follow-up study, mostly because of declined participation or an inability to contact. Thus, 1,218 ALPS participants and 436 STAN participants were enrolled in the follow-up study between October 2017 and August 2022. Of the 1,218 ALPS participants enrolled, 614 (50.4%) were exposed to betamethasone and 604 (49.6%) to placebo. Children of ALPS participants compared with ALPS nonparticipants in the follow-up study were older and had parents who were less likely to smoke during pregnancy and more likely to have private insurance and a college degree ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Of those in the follow-up study, maternal and neonatal characteristics were similar between those who received betamethasone and those who received placebo ( ). In addition, the follow-up cohort had a similar decrease in neonatal respiratory disease when exposed to betamethasone compared with placebo ( ). Of the 1,218 ALPS participants enrolled, 1,194 successfully completed spirometry (98.0%). There were no differences in the proportions meeting the primary composite outcome of childhood respiratory impairment (35.3% in the betamethasone group and 35.8% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 1.02, 95% CI, 0.87–1.18) or the individual components of the primary outcome ( ). Interaction terms of treatment assignment with private insurance, cesarean delivery, or sex were not significant. Children who had been exposed to betamethasone were less likely to have ever had wheezing or whistling in the chest (40.7% vs 45.5% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 0.88, 95% CI, 0.77–0.996, P =.04), although there were no differences in other evaluated outcomes ( ). Results for the association between betamethasone exposure and the primary outcome did not change in sensitivity analyses that used varied outcome assumptions for participants lost to follow-up or when the analysis was limited to children with postbronchodilator measurements ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Of those enrolled in the follow-up study, 771 ALPS participants (63.3%) and 251 STAN participants (57.6%) provided urine for cotinine immunoassay. Of the 973 valid samples, 210 ALPS participants (28.6%) and 81 STAN participants (33.9%) had urine cotinine levels suggestive of exposure to secondhand smoke. The reliability of parent-reported smoking in the household was low compared with urine cotinine levels (Cronbach α=0.60). Of the 291 participants with evidence of secondhand smoke exposure, 59.5% did not report smoking in the household. Results for the primary outcome did not change when the cohort was limited to children with urine cotinine measurements ( , http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). The sensitivity analysis that used inverse probability weighting to adjust for differences in maternal age, private insurance, and smoking status during pregnancy did not alter the estimates, and none of the primary or secondary outcomes changed significance. The primary outcome remained similar between the groups (36.0% in the betamethasone group and 36.7% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 1.01, 95% CI, 0.85–1.16). In addition, children who had been exposed to betamethasone were less likely to have ever had wheezing or whistling in the chest (41.2% compared with 45.7% in the placebo group, adjusted RR 0.88, 95% CI, 0.77–0.997) ( , available online at http://links.lww.com/AOG/E468 ). Childhood respiratory outcomes among children of ALPS participants were also compared with those of children of STAN participants. The STAN children in the follow-up study compared with the ALPS children in the follow-up study were older at follow-up, had been born at later gestational ages, were less likely to have had small-for-gestational-age birth weights, and had higher BMIs; their parents were less likely to have had a cesarean delivery. In addition, parents of STAN children were younger, less likely to have a college degree, and more likely to have private insurance or to identify as Black compared with parents of ALPS children exposed to betamethasone ( ). Of the 436 STAN participants enrolled, 432 successfully completed spirometry (99.1%). Given that the betamethasone group did not differ from the placebo group on the primary outcome, a noninferiority analysis comparing the betamethasone group with the term STAN cohort was no longer the ideal statistical analysis to perform. Given that the betamethasone group did not differ from the placebo group on the primary outcome, a noninferiority analysis comparing the betamethasone group with the term STAN cohort was no longer the ideal statistical analysis to perform. Comparisons were first made with children born to ALPS participants who had been randomized to the betamethasone group. The proportions meeting the primary composite outcome were 30.8% in the STAN group and 35.3% in the betamethasone group (adjusted RR 1.13, 95% CI, 0.94–1.36). The individual components of the primary outcome were not different by group ( ). The percent change in predicted FEV 1 was significantly lower among those in the betamethasone group (–0.4±14.3 in the betamethasone group and 1.9±9.9 in the STAN group, adjusted mean difference −2.69, 95% CI, −5.37 to −0.01). Wheezing during or after exercise in the past year was also significantly more likely in the betamethasone group (7.2% in the betamethasone group and 4.4% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.77, 95% CI, 1.03–3.06). Because a noninferiority analysis was initially planned, the adjusted risk difference of −3.6% (95% CI, −9.6 to 2.5%) for the primary outcome was also calculated, indicating that the betamethasone group is inferior to the STAN term cohort as anticipated given the lack of treatment difference between the betamethasone and placebo groups. Children of ALPS participants in the placebo group were also compared with children of STAN participants. Similar to the results from the comparison with the betamethasone group, there were no differences in the proportions meeting the primary composite outcome of childhood respiratory impairment (35.8% in the placebo group and 30.8% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.12, 95% CI, 0.94–1.33) or the individual components of the primary outcome ( , available online at http://links.lww . com/AOG/E468). Ever having wheezing or whistling in the chest (45.5% in the placebo group and 36.7% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 1.21, 95% CI, 1.03–1. 41) and wheezing during or after exercise in the past year were significantly higher in the placebo group (8. 8% in the placebo group and 4.4% in the STAN group, adjusted RR 2.09, 95% CI, 1.25–3.48). The individual components of abnormal spirometry are summarized by group in . DISCUSSION We found that late preterm antenatal corticosteroid exposure in pregnant individuals at risk of preterm birth did not influence the majority of childhood respiratory outcomes but did lower the frequency of ever having wheezing or whistling in the chest in their children aged 6 years or older. These data provide some insight into the trajectory of pulmonary maturation after late preterm birth and are the only data available on pulmonary outcomes after random allocation to betamethasone or placebo in the late preterm period. We also have found that, regardless of betamethasone exposure, children born to individuals at risk of late preterm birth have a greater risk of wheezing during or after exercise in the past year compared with those born at term in the STAN reference cohort. It is known that late preterm offspring have poorer respiratory outcomes compared with term offspring. , Todisco et al compared children born from 34 to 36 weeks of gestation without respiratory complications at birth with their term siblings by performing pulmonary function testing at a mean age of 11.6 years. They found that the preterm-born children had significantly increased residual volume and residual volume to total lung capacity compared with their term siblings. Similarly, Boyle et al found that children who had been born in the late preterm period had a higher risk of asthma and wheezing compared with their term counterparts. No studies have evaluated whether late preterm administration of betamethasone may improve long-term respiratory outcomes, and the available literature on earlier preterm betamethasone and long-term respiratory outcomes is mixed. An epidemiologic study of administrative data by Pole et al found an increased risk of asthma in children of pregnant individuals exposed to antenatal corticosteroids. The authors did not comment on the gestational age of exposure to steroids. Hung and colleagues sought to assess whether the frequencies of asthma and pulmonary dysfunction in children who were born preterm before 32 weeks of gestation with birth weights less than 1,500 g and who did not have neonatal bronchopulmonary dysplasia were related to antenatal corticosteroid exposure. After adjusting for confounders, including gestational age at delivery, they demonstrated a decrease in the rate of asthma after antenatal corticosteroid exposure (odds ratio 0.27, 95% CI, 0.08–0.88). Finally, follow-up of children whose birthing

of pregnant individuals exposed to antenatal corticosteroids. The authors did not comment on the gestational age of exposure to steroids. Hung and colleagues sought to assess whether the frequencies of asthma and pulmonary dysfunction in children who were born preterm before 32 weeks of gestation with birth weights less than 1,500 g and who did not have neonatal bronchopulmonary dysplasia were related to antenatal corticosteroid exposure. After adjusting for confounders, including gestational age at delivery, they demonstrated a decrease in the rate of asthma after antenatal corticosteroid exposure (odds ratio 0.27, 95% CI, 0.08–0.88). Finally, follow-up of children whose birthing parents had been enrolled in the term steroids ASTECS (Antenatal Steroids for Term Elective Caesarean Section) trial did not find a difference in rates of childhood asthma between exposure groups. Our findings are similar to the findings in the ASTECS follow-up. Furthermore, by comparing children from the ALPS trial, 84.3% of whom were born late preterm, with children from the STAN trial, all of whom were born at term, we have shown that wheezing during or after exercise in the past year was more common in the ALPS group. There are a few notable limitations of our findings. We enrolled just more than half of the intended sample size of 2,000 participants, likely because of both the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and the difficulty finding parent trial participants. There is also the possibility of self-selection bias because those who participated in the follow-up study significantly differed from those who did not. However, results of the sensitivity analysis using inverse probability weighting to approximate the full ALPS cohort demonstrated similar results. Secondary outcomes may have also been affected by recall bias because they were reported by the caregiver. We initially estimated a primary outcome rate of 16.0%. With an increased primary outcome rate of 35.0% in the placebo group, our final sample size gave us more than 90.0% power to show either a 30.0% relative decrease (35.0–24.5%) or 30.0% relative increase (35.0–45.5%) in the primary outcome. The initial protocol included postspirometry bronchodilation with albuterol, but this procedure had to be abandoned during the pandemic because of the multiple-use vials and concern for spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). However, examining the data of the participants enrolled before the pandemic who provided postspirometry data did not change our results. Lastly, secondary outcomes were exploratory and thus may have been underpowered. In addition, because there was no adjustment for multiple comparisons, several secondary findings are possibly attributable to chance. The study also has several strengths. It is the only follow-up study of respiratory outcomes after late preterm administration of betamethasone compared with placebo, and it is one of the largest follow-up studies of single-course corticosteroids at any gestational age. Spirometry was performed with central oversight by trained research personnel, and almost all tests provided usable results. The use of a term-born reference cohort allowed us to compare outcomes with those born at term who were not at risk of late preterm birth. Research staff, participants, and investigators remained blinded to treatment assignment, minimizing bias in outcome assessment. In conclusion, administration of late preterm antenatal corticosteroids improved short-term respiratory outcomes but did not affect childhood pulmonary outcomes, aside from ever having less wheezing or whistling in the chest, compared with those exposed to placebo. documents.title: SMFM Consult Series 62 Best Practices in Equitable Care Delivery in Maternal-Fetal Medicine

chunks.content: Introduction The association between systemic racism and adverse health outcomes is a key driver of racial and ethnic health disparities. , Discrimination, a measurable manifestation of structural racism, is a recognized source of stress associated with numerous adverse health outcomes. Observational data link higher levels of reported discrimination with hypertension, cigarette use, inflammation, atherosclerosis, negative physical and mental health, and higher mortality. , Discrimination is also a factor in the disproportionate impact of the current maternal health crisis on historically marginalized communities: high levels of perceived discrimination have been associated with risk of very low birthweight, increased stress markers during pregnancy, decreased postpartum care attendance, less control of health choices, and increased risk of gestational diabetes. - Individual experience with discrimination may also play a role in contraceptive choice; - higher reported levels of discrimination are associated with lower birth control use and more use of highly-effective methods among those who are using contraception. , However, previous studies have not assessed the impact of discrimination on contraceptive choice among postpartum patients. Given the documented impact of discrimination during pregnancy, the postpartum period could be a time when discrimination has a particularly strong impact on contraceptive choice. Alternatively, other factors may me more influential in postpartum contraceptive choice such as structural barriers to contraceptive access, disparities in counseling, and disparate desire for contraception may influence contraceptive choice. , , We sought to measure discrimination in healthcare among a group of individuals postpartum prior to hospital discharge and assess whether discrimination was associated with their postpartum contraceptive plan. We hypothesized that those reporting higher levels of discrimination would be less likely to plan to use most effective and moderately effective contraception. Methods Settings and study procedures Our study was conducted at an academic, tertiary care hospital in North Carolina. Between June 2021 and January 2023, we approached inpatient individuals during their postpartum stay and asked them to complete a 10-minute electronic survey. We included those who were at least 18 years old, were English or Spanish speaking and were recovering on the postpartum floor. We excluded those who had a fetal or neonatal demise, who had undergone hysterectomy or who were admitted in a different hospital setting such as the intensive care unit. Our hospital offers both immediate postpartum permanent contraception procedures and immediate postpartum LARC. Participants were approached and enrolled by a study coordinator and then completed the survey on a tablet device. They received compensation for their time. The survey included the Perceived Discrimination in Healthcare Scale, self-reported information about race and ethnicity, income, household size, transportation challenges, Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC), and home ownership. We also asked about their contraceptive plan, and how they would like to be contacted in the future. Obstetric and health variables were abstracted from the chart by a study coordinator. Exposures The primary exposure was the patient’s perceived discrimination in health care setting. We measured this using the previously validated 7-item scale. The measure has the common prompt, “When getting healthcare, have any of the following things happened to you because of your race or color?” We asked an eighth question, “Do you feel you received poorer services than other people by staff outside your provider such as the receptionist, security guard or scheduler?” to assess experiences not focused on healthcare provider interactions. We thought these experiences could be important to patient perceptions of care and they were not captured in the original scale. Possible responses for each question indicated the participant experienced something “never”, “once”, “two to three times”, and “four or more times”. We used Cronbach’s alpha to assess whether the scale was internally consistent with inclusion of this item. To create a total sum score, each question in the seven-item original scale was dichotomized giving zero points for “never experienced/experienced once” or one point for “two or three times” or “four or more times.” We combined never experienced and experienced once because we hypothesized that multiple exposures to discrimination in healthcare would be more likely to alter behavior. We then summed across seven questions yielding a total score ranging from zero to seven. We dichotomized the total perceived discrimination sum score to compare those who did not report perceived discrimination in healthcare or had one experience versus those who reported multiple discriminatory experiences. We conducted a sensitivity analysis in which we graded individual questions from zero to three points based on the number of reported episodes of discrimination, as described above. We then calculated a total sum score and compared those reporting those who experienced two or more episodes of discrimination overall, versus those who never experienced/experienced once discrimination. Because this is a study of perceived racial discrimination, we report on and analyze by self-reported race and ethnicity. Outcomes Our primary outcome was planned tier

did not report perceived discrimination in healthcare or had one experience versus those who reported multiple discriminatory experiences. We conducted a sensitivity analysis in which we graded individual questions from zero to three points based on the number of reported episodes of discrimination, as described above. We then calculated a total sum score and compared those reporting those who experienced two or more episodes of discrimination overall, versus those who never experienced/experienced once discrimination. Because this is a study of perceived racial discrimination, we report on and analyze by self-reported race and ethnicity. Outcomes Our primary outcome was planned tier of postpartum contraceptive efficacy including most effective, moderately effective and least effective. We also reported those who said they were undecided or planned not to use contraception. Most effective methods included tubal ligation, IUD, implant, vasectomy; moderately effective methods included pills, ring, patch, injection; less effective methods included condoms, diaphragm, withdrawal, and natural family planning. We did not query about planned use of lactational amenorrhea. Participants could select "I will not use birth control" or provided text explanation for "Other". A subset of participants wrote "Undecided" or "Unsure". Participants who selected “Other” without providing additional information or did not answer the question regarding contraceptive plan were excluded from analysis. To test if there is an association between the perceived discrimination and contraceptive plan effectiveness tier, a Chi-square test was performed. Sample size We planned to recruit 500 participants. We anticipated we would need N=462 participants to detect a 15% difference in planned contraceptive efficacy tier between those with low and high discrimination scores with 90% power and a two-sided alpha of 0.05. Statistical analysis Patient characteristics including demographics, obstetric history, and self-reported social characteristics were summarized by the dichotomized perceived discrimination (never vs once or more). Continuous variables were summarized using mean (standard deviation, SD) or median (Q1, Q3) while categorical variables were summarized as frequency (percentage). To assess whether patient characteristics were associated with planned postpartum contraceptive efficacy tier (excluding “Undecided”), ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to compare differences between groups for continuous variables. Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests were used for categorical variables. To investigate the association between perceived discrimination and contraceptive efficacy tier, multinomial logistic regression model was used with “most effective” as the reference level. This model was fit with and without covariates including age, race, number of living children, payor, and own a home. We conducted a sensitivity analysis including educational attainment in the model. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. All analyses were performed in SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC) at a two-tailed, 5% level of significance. The Duke University Health System Institutional Review Board approved this study. Results A total of n=773 individuals were deemed eligible and approached to participate, . Among approached individuals, 64.7% agreed to participate. A total of n=500 individuals completed the survey though nine were excluded from analysis because they did not sign the consent form and an additional nine were excluded who did not answer about their contraceptive plan, leaving a total of n=482 participants. We excluded individuals with incomplete information on key variables or for sample sizes less than 10 in racial or ethnic categories for regression models (n=21). Participants had a mean age of 30.6 (SD 5.7) and most had at least one living child aside from the current birth (61.4%, ). Almost two-thirds of patients had a body mass index (BMI) > or equal to 30 at the time of delivery (65.7%). Participants were racially and ethnically diverse with the highest proportions reporting Black (36.1%), White (43.4%) or Asian (7.3%) race, and 10.2% reporting Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Most patients used private commercial insurance, Tricare or VA insurance (63.5%) while many used Medicaid or Medicare (34.6%). Most patients had incomes >200% of the federal poverty level when adjusted for family size (53.5%). A minority owned a home (40.7%), used WIC during pregnancy (39.4%), or reported transportation challenges impacted medical care (5.2%). Overall, 78.6% of participants had no or few discrimination experiences while 21.4% had multiple discrimination experiences ( ). Race was associated with higher frequency of discrimination with 52.4% of those reporting discrimination being Black (p<0.001). Participants most commonly reported experiences in which a doctor or nurse was not listening to them (17.9%) or a doctor or nurse acted as though they were not smart (12.3%). The item we added querying discrimination by non-medical personnel was positive among 7.7% of participants. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.92 with an without inclusion of the eight item demonstrating excellent internal consistency. Delivery characteristics including median gestational age (38 weeks, IQR 37, 39), preterm birth status (15.8%) and cesarean rate (43.2%) were similar among those who did and did not have multiple discrimination experiences ( ). Infant NICU admission was correlated with having

commonly reported experiences in which a doctor or nurse was not listening to them (17.9%) or a doctor or nurse acted as though they were not smart (12.3%). The item we added querying discrimination by non-medical personnel was positive among 7.7% of participants. Cronbach’s alpha was 0.92 with an without inclusion of the eight item demonstrating excellent internal consistency. Delivery characteristics including median gestational age (38 weeks, IQR 37, 39), preterm birth status (15.8%) and cesarean rate (43.2%) were similar among those who did and did not have multiple discrimination experiences ( ). Infant NICU admission was correlated with having had multiple experiences of discrimination (multiple vs no or few N=29/103, 28.2% vs N=62/379, 16.4%, p=0.007). The positive association between NICU admission and multiple episodes of discrimination remained statistically significant in a model adjusting for Black race (aOR 1.56; 95% CI 1.06-2.32). Correlates with postpartum contraceptive plan Overall, 43.0% of participants planned to use a most effective and 29.7% planned to use a moderately effective contraceptive method ( ). Fewer participants planned to use less effective methods (13.1%), planned not to use birth control (14.2%), or said they were undecided (2.1%). In bivariate comparison, a number of demographic variables were associated with planned contraceptive use. Contraceptive plan significantly differed by age, race, number of living children, insurance payor, federal poverty status, home ownership and WIC use during pregnancy ( ). Having had multiple experiences of perceived discrimination in healthcare was not significantly associated with planned contraceptive use (p=0.371). We constructed a multivariable model to assess the association between perceived discrimination and postpartum contraceptive efficacy including age, race, number of living children, insurance payor, and whether the participant owned a home. Perceived discrimination was not significantly associated with efficacy tier of planned postpartum contraception. However, we observed increasing odds for less effective contraceptive method (adjusted OR 1.46, 95%CI 0.71-2.66) or not to use contraception (adjusted OR 1.42, 95%CI 0.74-2.73) among those with multiple experiences of discrimination though not statistically significant. ( ) Sensitivity analyses With our alternative approach to the perceived discrimination scale, an additional 31 individuals would have been included in our exposed group. We did not observe a significant association between perceived discrimination and contraceptive plan ( ). The observed relationship between NICU admission and perceived discrimination adjusting for Black race was no longer statistically significant (aOR 1.28, 95%CI 0.86, 1.88). Additionally, inclusion of educational attainment in the multivariable model did not change our interpretation of the results ( ). Discussion Among a diverse group of postpartum participants, we found that higher levels of perceived discrimination in healthcare were not significantly associated with planned tier of postpartum contraceptive efficacy. Our finding that a sizeable proportion of patients reported multiple episodes of discrimination in their medical care (N=103, 21.4%) warrants intervention, regardless of whether discrimination is associated with contraceptive outcomes. Contraceptive decision-making is complex and highly personal. Our results demonstrate a relatively high proportion of individuals planning to use contraception in the most (43.0%) and moderately (29.7%) effective tiers. At the population level, observed differences in contraceptive choice among racial and ethnic groups are shaped by a variety of factors, including disparate geographic access to contraception, cost barriers disproportionately experienced by historically minoritized populations, historic and contemporary coercive practices especially around permanent contraception and LARC, social network experiences and norms, and individual personal preferences. - Many of these components of systemic racism may directly or indirectly influence how patients experience interactions with health care providers and health systems. Our results suggest that experiences of discrimination in the healthcare setting may be less important than these other factors in shaping contraceptive choice among postpartum patients. Examination of the role of discrimination in postpartum contraceptive choice is warranted because patients experience racial discrimination in family planning encounters and prior studies have found an association between higher levels of discrimination and non-use of contraception. , Contraceptive counseling is a particularly important example of shared decision-making, and perceived discrimination has been shown to play a role in outcomes of the shared decision-making process in other clinical areas. - Regardless of their ultimate choice of method, patients who feel pressured around contraception or whose actions differ from their providers’ recommendations report higher levels of perceived discrimination. Although the results from our multivariable model indicating increased odds of less effective or no contraception among those reporting discrimination did not achieve statistical significance, they do suggest provider communication as a potentially helpful intervention target. We observed a similar prevalence of race and ethnicity-based perceived discrimination in healthcare (21.4%) as other studies, even given use of different measures and heterogenous interpretation of those measures. , , - In our study, the two most commonly reported domains in which participants reported discrimination were related to provider-patient communication: that participants felt a doctor or nurse was not listening to what

discrimination. Although the results from our multivariable model indicating increased odds of less effective or no contraception among those reporting discrimination did not achieve statistical significance, they do suggest provider communication as a potentially helpful intervention target. We observed a similar prevalence of race and ethnicity-based perceived discrimination in healthcare (21.4%) as other studies, even given use of different measures and heterogenous interpretation of those measures. , , - In our study, the two most commonly reported domains in which participants reported discrimination were related to provider-patient communication: that participants felt a doctor or nurse was not listening to what they were saying (18%), and that a doctor or nurse acted as though the patient was not smart (12%). In our setting, addressing and improving patient-provider communication may be an important step in reducing one component of structural racism in healthcare. Communication training is recognized as a useful corollary to institutional or health systems efforts to reduce racial health disparities. Education efforts cannot be restricted to providers such as doctors and nurses as patients encounter a variety of individuals in receipt of health care. Our study included an eight item to assess discrimination from non-medical personnel. Inclusion was based on prior data demonstrating this may be an important and previously unassessed source of negative interactions for patients and our data suggest inclusion may be warranted in future studies. Disparities in contraceptive access are often identified as one mediator of racial, ethnic and socioeconomic disparities in risk of unintended pregnancy. Unintended pregnancy is, in turn, a driver of adverse health, economic and social outcomes especially given the risks of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes with short interval pregnancy. , If systemic racism increases the likelihood of unintended pregnancy by contributing to higher use of less effective methods, it actually helps perpetuate ongoing disparities in health, economic, and social outcomes. The postpartum period is considered a key time for making contraceptive choices because of high healthcare engagement, insurance coverage, and readiness and receptivity to counseling. , Therefore, interventions to reduce systemic racism during pregnancy and the postpartum period could potentially decrease the risk of subsequent unintended pregnancy and affect a number of outcomes, even in light of the null results in the current study. - Limitations of this study include our inability to isolate when patients experienced discrimination as the survey did not ask whether it occurred during this pregnancy or obstetric care. This measurement tool also does not assess the level of stress discriminatory experiences caused, which probably ranged for different participants. The perceived discrimination scale used in this study focuses on interpersonal interactions rather than systemic racism such as access to healthcare, education and just financial systems. While we conducted a priori power analyses, we ultimately had relatively small numbers of patients who planned to use less effective methods or no contraception, limiting statistical power. We might have had greater power had we scored the perceived discrimination scale continuously, though our sensitivity analysis suggests it would be unlikely to affect the results. Our data is from a single institution, which may limit generalizability. In our setting, contraceptive counseling and content are not standardized and counseling often occurs during prenatal care, inpatient and postpartum periods. Documentation of the contraceptive plan is part of the discharge template which may prompt inpatient discussion. Non-standardized counseling is a strength of this study because counseling timing, content and delivery could all influence how counseling is perceived. Another strength of this study is that planned contraception was assessed directly from participants in our survey, not via chart review. Planned contraception at the time of discharge may differ from actual use because of fluidity in preference, barriers to access, and subsequent experience after hospital discharge—including dissatisfaction with contraception. - Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first assessment of perceived discrimination in healthcare among postpartum individuals inpatient prior to discharge. The puerperium is a critical time period for contraceptive choice and future health. Our findings did not rule out an association between discrimination and the choice of a less effective method or no contraception. As one in five participants reported discrimination in healthcare, systemic issues that allow these experiences to persist should be examined. Systemic racism and interpersonal perceived discrimination may work in tandem to exacerbate disparate outcomes. Further studies in the postpartum setting with larger sample sizes are warranted, particularly since our findings suggest that provider-patient communication factors, which are relatively easy to address compared to components of systemic racism, are a major driver of perceived discrimination. documents.title: SMFM Consult Series 64 Sickle Cell Disease in Pregnancy

chunks.content: Introduction Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy and the most common inherited, clinically significant blood disorder. , Pregnant individuals with SCD have an increased risk of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. However, prepregnancy counseling and multidisciplinary care can lead to favorable maternal and neonatal outcomes. High-level evidence to guide SCD management in pregnancy is sparse. This consult series presents the best available evidence to manage this complex disease process during pregnancy and outlines opportunities for research to help enhance available evidence for future advances in perinatal SCD care. What are the pathophysiologic and epidemiologic characteristics of sickle cell disease? SCD occurs as a result of a single amino acid change of glutamic acid to valine in the beta-globin subunit of hemoglobin. In stressful environments in those with SCD, red blood cells (RBCs) polymerize into a more elongated sickle or S shape prone to hemolysis, endothelial adhesion, and subsequent vaso-occlusion. Approximately 100,000 persons in the United States have SCD; globally, approximately 300,000 neonates are born with SCD each year. SCD is particularly common among people whose ancestors came from sub-Saharan Africa; Spanish-speaking regions in the Western Hemisphere (South America, the Caribbean, and Central America); Saudi Arabia; India; and Mediterranean countries (Turkey, Greece, and Italy). In the United States, 1 in 365 neonates described as African American or Black are diagnosed with SCD. Importantly, race should not be used in isolation as an assessment for genetic risk. Several genotypes result in the phenotypic expression of SCD. The most common form in the United States is homozygous S or HbSS disease. Other common genotypes include the compound heterozygotes of HbS beta plus thalassemia (HbS β +), HbS beta null thalassemia (HbS β 0 ), and HbSC. Although people with HbSS and HbS β 0 often experience a more severe clinical course, individuals with all types of SCD are at risk of severe complications. - If 2 unaffected carriers of an S allele (sickle cell trait [SCT]) produce an offspring, the offspring has a 25% chance of being unaffected (not a carrier), a 50% chance to be a carrier, and a 25% chance to have SCD. Who should be screened for sickle cell disease? In 1996, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommended screening for SCD in all newborns. By 2006, newborn screening was required and implemented in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. However, people with SCT, thalassemia trait, or hemoglobin C disease may be unaware of their status. As recommended by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, all patients presenting for prepregnancy or prenatal care should be offered a complete blood count (CBC) with RBC indices and hemoglobin electrophoresis testing. Those diagnosed with SCT or disease should have their partner undergo hemoglobinopathy evaluation to assess the risk of SCD or other hemoglobinopathies to their offspring. How is sickle cell disease diagnosed? The recommended laboratory techniques for detecting hemoglobinopathies are hemoglobin electrophoresis and DNA molecular testing. , Genetic testing of the beta-globin gene is the most accurate method of diagnosis, but it requires a specialized laboratory, is more expensive, and is usually reserved for special situations (i.e., conflicting protein method results). The methods that only test for the presence of sickle cells (e.g., sickle cell prep) do not detect non–S hemoglobin variants and are inadequate to distinguish between SCT, SCD, and compound heterozygous states, such as HbSC disease. There are many expanded carrier screening panels that evaluate for hemoglobinopathies; however, the preferred tests for the diagnosis of SCD or trait are a CBC with RBC indices and a hemoglobin electrophoresis. What are the manifestations of sickle cell disease? Vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis occur at baseline resulting in anemia, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation. Repeated episodes of vaso-occlusion, hemolysis, and anemia can cause chronic organ complications for individuals with SCD ( ). When vaso-occlusion results in tissue ischemia, this is commonly called a “vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)” or “acute painful episode.” VOCs are acute painful complications of SCD and the most commonly reported reason individuals with SCD present to emergency departments. Vaso-occlusive episodes cost the US healthcare system more than $800 million in 2016. Patients typically present with severe back, chest, or extremity pain. In general, triggers may include infection, extreme temperatures, dehydration, acidosis, and hypoxia; however, the specific triggers for a VOC are often unknown. Isolated vaso-occlusive events characterized by pain without evidence of organ dysfunction are referred to as uncomplicated VOC. In contrast, a complicated VOC refers to pain in addition to an acute organ-based complication of SCD, such as acute chest syndrome (ACS), stroke, hepatic or splenic sequestration, or osteomyelitis. Other acute complications of SCD are presented in . What is the life expectancy of a person with sickle cell disease? Chronic organ complications, such as renal and cardiopulmonary disease, along with ACS, are the leading

Isolated vaso-occlusive events characterized by pain without evidence of organ dysfunction are referred to as uncomplicated VOC. In contrast, a complicated VOC refers to pain in addition to an acute organ-based complication of SCD, such as acute chest syndrome (ACS), stroke, hepatic or splenic sequestration, or osteomyelitis. Other acute complications of SCD are presented in . What is the life expectancy of a person with sickle cell disease? Chronic organ complications, such as renal and cardiopulmonary disease, along with ACS, are the leading causes of death for adults with SCD. Advances in management have drastically increased the life span of persons with SCD. With the introduction of universal newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis for children with SCD, and hydroxyurea, among other interventions, persons in the United States with SCD have a median life expectancy of 58 years. Since 1980, the life expectancy of persons with SCD has more than doubled, significantly increasing the prevalence of reproductive-aged women and pregnancy in this special population. What adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes are associated with sickle cell disease in pregnancy? Pregnancies in patients with SCD are associated with adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Mortality is significantly increased in pregnant patients with SCD compared with pregnant patients without SCD. Worldwide maternal mortality for those with SCD has increased 10- to 18-fold compared with those without SCD, with risk attenuated to a 3- to 4-fold increase in high-income countries. , ACS and pneumonia occur in 6.5% of pregnant women with SCD, with pulmonary causes contributing to 88% of maternal deaths in patients with SCD. Severe morbidities are associated with SCD in pregnancy, including bacterial infections (odds ratio [OR], 2.48), pulmonary thromboembolism (relative risk [RR], 7.74), and pulmonary hypertension (OR, 6.3). In addition, obstetrical complications are increased in pregnant patients with SCD, including preeclampsia (RR, 2.06), eclampsia (OR, 3.02), cesarean delivery (OR, 1.54), abruption (OR, 1.6), and preterm labor (OR, 1.4). Perinatal risks are similarly increased in pregnancies complicated by SCD, including fetal growth restriction (OR, 2.79), low birthweight (OR, 2.00), small-for-gestational-age neonate (RR, 3.72), and preterm birth (RR, 2.21). Moreover, risks of stillbirth (OR, 4.05) and neonatal death (OR, 2.71) are increased. In addition, individuals with SCD may be burdened by conditions, such as fatigue, depression, and anxiety, that negatively affect their quality of life and emotional well-being. These conditions may potentially be exacerbated during pregnancy and the postpartum period. Which patients with sickle cell disease face the highest risk of mortality associated with pregnancy? Pregnant patients with SCD have an increased risk of maternal and perinatal complications, including death. Given the unequivocal increased risk of maternal morbidity and mortality, reproductive options (including abortion) should be discussed with all pregnant patients with SCD. - Patients with SCD should be supported in making an informed decision regarding their reproductive options in a shared decision-making process in consultation with maternal-fetal medicine (MFM) subspecialists and hematologists with expertise in SCD, as appropriate. Most pregnant patients will have a successful outcome; however, there are certain patients with SCD in whom pregnancy significantly increases the risk of maternal death. Specifically, pulmonary hypertension and significant cardiomyopathies classified as modified World Health Organization class IV diseases are contraindications to pregnancy. In addition, the inability to receive blood products because of severe alloimmunization and lack of available matched blood and other rare and severe complications of SCD that confer additional risks of morbidity and mortality (e.g., moyamoya syndrome) should be identified and incorporated into individualized counseling with a high degree of caution against attempting or continuing a pregnancy. What is the prepregnancy and pregnancy management for a patient with sickle cell disease? There are 4 general categories of evaluation and counseling for the patient with SCD who is pregnant or contemplating pregnancy: prepregnancy counseling, baseline maternal assessment, medication assessment, and genetic counseling. We recommend that patients with SCD be managed by a multidisciplinary team that includes maternal-fetal medicine, hematology (ideally a hematologist specializing in SCD), genetics, pain management, and social work or behavioral health (as appropriate) starting in early pregnancy (Best Practice). - What prepregnancy and early pregnancy care specific to sickle cell disease should be provided? Prepregnancy counseling Prepregnancy counseling allows a patient with SCD the opportunity to make an informed decision regarding pregnancy after consideration of the maternal and fetal risks and the potential risks to the offspring. Reproductive planning options that reduce fetal risks include preimplantation genetics and using donor egg or sperm (screened for hemoglobinopathies). However, in vitro fertilization and donor egg or sperm are associated with a myriad of maternal risks, including preeclampsia and neonatal risks, including prematurity. - Reproductive planning options that mitigate maternal risk for individuals with SCD include surrogacy and adoption. Referrals to MFM, genetics, and reproductive endocrinology specialists, as appropriate, should be made in the prepregnancy period depending on individualized reproductive planning needs and desires. In addition, this is an opportunity to educate patients about disease management and prenatal genetic counseling and testing options, which may improve informed decision-making, healthcare utilization, and rates of depression associated with SCD. Prepregnancy counseling for patients with SCD should include baseline maternal assessment, medication assessment, and genetic counseling, as described in detail below. Baseline maternal assessment A thorough history should be obtained, including an assessment of previous SCD complications and current medications. Laboratory evaluation includes assessing for anemia, evaluating iron stores, obtaining a type and screen to assess for alloimmunization, and assessing thoroughly end-organ function, as outlined in . Understanding a patient’s current health status aids in counseling regarding the likelihood of pregnancy complications. For example, a patient without end-organ damage and previous uncomplicated term deliveries incurs a different level of risk in pregnancy compared with a patient with severe anemia on hydroxyurea with a history of ACS. Patients with SCD should be optimized and comanaged by a hematologist who is up to date on health maintenance screening according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) and American Society of Hematology (ASH) , , , , guidelines. Ideally, health maintenance should be optimized before pregnancy. For patients with a lapse in care, pregnancy represents a unique window for heightened adherence and, for some, access to healthcare that they did not have before. Therefore, referrals for SCD management should be expedited during pregnancy. A transition from pediatric specialty care to adult specialty care may be needed, particularly for young patients with SCD previously managed by pediatric hematologists. Baseline medication assessment Many individuals with SCD are on several medications for disease treatment and pain management. Many medications may be safely continued during pregnancy, whereas others should be switched to a safer alternative or discontinued. outlines common medications used in SCD management and principles of management for the pregnant patient. Recommendations regarding medication continuation must account for the patient’s disease severity and desires after discussing risks, benefits, and alternatives. New evidence emerges regularly; referencing perinatal medication databases such as Reprotox ® , may provide current information on specific drug risks for individualized counseling. Genetic counseling All patients with SCD should be offered genetic counseling, ideally before pregnancy, to be informed of their risk of having offspring who are carriers or affected with SCD. Key components of genetic counseling include disease characterization (i.e., HbSS, HBSC, and HbS β +) for both patient and partner. Individuals who are at risk of having a child with SCD and present for prepregnancy counseling should be informed about alternative reproductive options. Patients with SCD who present during pregnancy should also be offered genetic counseling and informed of the risk of having a child born with SCD, along with screening and testing options (including newborn screening) for the current pregnancy. Antenatal diagnostic options, including chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis should be offered. Newer noninvasive (cell-free DNA) screening tests that report the fetal risk of SCD are commercially available, , but not currently recommended in pregnancy. If, despite this, a patient undergoes screening with positive cell-free DNA screening results for SCD, confirmatory diagnosis should be offered. If not performed antenatally, the diagnosis can be confirmed postnatally. What vaccinations should patients with sickle cell disease receive in pregnancy? Pregnant patients with SCD should receive all routinely recommended antenatal vaccinations. - Patients can be reassured that the COVID-19 vaccines currently available in the United States do not appear to increase the rates of VOC. Additional vaccines, which should be administered (if due) during pregnancy for patients with SCD, include meningococcal vaccination (MenACWY) every 5 years and pneumococcal vaccination (PPSV23) ≥5 years after the first dose. It is important to remember that many pregnant patients have significant barriers to care, and pregnancy may represent a unique window whereby patients have access to lifesaving immunizations. We recommend that pregnant patients with SCD receive all routinely recommended antenatal vaccinations in addition to meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccination if due (GRADE 1A). In addition to routine prenatal care, what additional items should be considered for the pregnant patient with sickle cell disease? Daily folic acid supplementation is recommended for pregnant patients with SCD. RBC turnover occurs more frequently in patients with SCD (and other hemolytic anemias), and folic acid supplementation repletes folate stores needed for hematopoiesis. Similar to all pregnant patients, prenatal vitamins are recommended for pregnant patients with SCD. However, iron-free prenatal vitamins should be the default for patients with SCD unless iron deficiency is documented. We recommend prenatal vitamins without iron unless iron deficiency is confirmed and initiation of 4 mg of folic acid for pregnant patients with SCD (GRADE 1B). , - Patients with SCD have an increased risk of urinary tract infections. - In addition to a baseline urine culture at the entry to prenatal care, many providers obtain urine cultures each trimester because of the increased risk of asymptomatic bacteriuria. Evidence to support this is lacking. However, a baseline urine culture at the initial prenatal visit and some form of urine assessment, such as dipstick or urinalysis, at each prenatal visit are suggested. Patients with SCD have an increased risk of vitamin D deficiency; therefore, checking a baseline vitamin D level is suggested. Repletion of vitamin D at 1000 to 2000 international units daily seems safe in pregnancy. What fetal surveillance is indicated for the pregnant patient with sickle cell disease? Pregnant patients with SCD should undergo an ultrasound when they present for prenatal care to confirm the presence of a viable intrauterine pregnancy and to reliably date the pregnancy. Early confirmation of an intrauterine pregnancy is important as this may affect medication management concerning teratogen exposure. A detailed anatomic survey should be performed ≥18 weeks of gestation to screen for congenital anomalies, particularly among patients taking potential teratogens immediately before or during the first trimester of pregnancy. Fetal growth surveillance by ultrasound is indicated given the increased risk of fetal growth restriction in patients with SCD. , , Severe forms of SCD, including HbSS and HbS β 0 disease, confer the greatest risk. We recommend fetal growth surveillance every 4 weeks beginning in the 28th week of gestation (GRADE 1C). Antenatal fetal surveillance is indicated for pregnant patients with an increased risk of stillbirth. A 2016 meta-analysis, including data from 9 countries, found that patients with SCD have a significantly increased risk of stillbirth with an OR of 4.05. In contrast, a contemporary statewide retrospective cohort study found no significant increase in stillbirth among women with SCD. The authors hypothesized that this finding reflected improved antenatal surveillance and management. It is unknown if third-trimester antenatal fetal surveillance reduces stillbirth risk in pregnancies complicated by SCD with normally grown fetuses; however, it is reasonable to consider antenatal fetal surveillance for all patients with SCD given the above RR for stillbirth and the unknown degree to which fetal growth restriction is responsible for the increase in risk. Patients with SCD and a growth-restricted fetus should be assigned to antenatal fetal surveillance according to guidelines for fetal growth restriction. , For patients with uncomplicated SCD and a normally-grown fetus, we suggest weekly or twice weekly antenatal testing beginning at 32 to 34 weeks of gestation. For patients with complicated SCD (i.e., maternal hypertension, VOC, fetal growth restriction, or other coexisting complication), we suggest initiating individualized antenatal testing at diagnosis or at a gestational age when delivery would be considered if results are abnormal (GRADE 2B). Other forms of SCD (e.g., hemoglobin SC disease) have less clear effects on the risk of perinatal death. , Therefore, in the absence of other complications, antenatal fetal surveillance for patients with hemoglobinopathies other than HbSS or HbS β 0 disease should be individualized and should take into account factors, such as fetal growth and disease severity. Individuals presenting with uncomplicated VOC (i.e., pain without evidence of organ dysfunction) are typically managed with oral or intravenous (IV) fluids and analgesic medications. Pain caused by an uncomplicated VOC may last up to 2 weeks. RBC transfusion is not recommended for uncomplicated VOC. , Providers should observe for acute complications of SCD in patients presenting with VOC and alter the management plan accordingly. Complicated VOC should be treated in collaboration with a hematologist and may require additional assessment, diagnostic evaluation, and RBC transfusion in addition to pain management. ACS deserves particular attention in the evaluation of VOC as it is the leading cause of death among patients with SCD. ACS is diagnosed by imaging findings consistent with a new pulmonary infiltrate and one additional item, which may include oxygen desaturation, cough, temperature of ≥101.3°F, tachypnea, or wheezing. , ACS should be kept on the differential diagnosis, and a hematologist, pulmonologist, or other SCD specialist should be consulted for prompt evaluation and treatment. The management of ACS includes pain control (at a dose that provides adequate pain control but avoids sedation), IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and blood transfusions to decrease HbS to <30%. , Incentive spirometry should be performed every 2 hours while the patient is awake. , How should a vaso-occlusive crisis be treated in pregnant patients? VOC in pregnant patients is initially treated with hydration and aggressive pain management. Oxygen need not be initiated unless O2 saturation levels are <95%, in which case additional pulmonary assessment is needed. The threshold for oxygen supplementation in the pregnant patient is lower than in the nonpregnant patient with SCD to maintain an effective gradient for fetal gas exchange. In addition, hydration should be administered, although the rate and volume of fluid administration must be balanced with risks of volume overload and pulmonary edema. Isotonic IV and oral fluids are preferred; hypertonic fluids are not recommended. In the patient with dehydration, fluids may be continued until clinical improvement. An evaluation for infectious etiology or trigger for VOC should be performed and treatment initiated as indicated and treated. The initial workup in pregnancy includes a CBC with differential, lactate dehydrogenase, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, and urine culture. Routine radiography is not needed. A chest radiograph should be obtained if the patient has respiratory symptoms, hypoxia, or a significant decrease in hemoglobin level. Patients should be treated with IV opioids for acute VOC according to their individualized pain plan (if present) or according to the ASH guideline on management of pain ( ). Anemia assessment is crucial for patients who present with a drop in hemoglobin level compared with their baseline. Although transfusion may be considered for those whose hemoglobin level is significantly lower than baseline depending on the clinical context, it is important to exclude causes of anemia other than splenic sequestration that might require different management strategies, such as hemolysis, acute bleeding, or ACS. Exchange transfusions are indicated in the acute setting for patients presenting with symptoms of acute ischemic stroke, severe ACS (or any cause of hypoxic respiratory failure), or multisystem organ failure. A hemoglobin electrophoresis may be obtained to determine the percentage of hemoglobin S but is not needed in the acute setting and can be estimated on the basis of the patient’s previous transfusion history. In general, the goal of an exchange transfusion is to decrease the abnormal hemoglobin level (HbS or HbS+C) to <30%. What principles of pain management should be utilized in managing a patient with sickle cell disease? Outside of pregnancy, individuals with SCD are ideally managed using principles of pain management outlined in the 2020 ASH guideline for SCD on the management of acute and chronic pain. With few exceptions, as outlined in , we recommend following evidence-based guidelines for the management of chronic and acute pain during pregnancy (Best Practice). summarizes key ASH recommendations and good practice statements for the management of acute and chronic pain (left column) and presents Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine pregnancy-specific modifications where applicable (right column). Shared decision-making should guide pain management in pregnant patients with SCD, and all patients should have an individualized pain management plan. Pregnant patients presenting with acute SCD pain should receive rapid assessment and administration of analgesia according to standard protocols and order sets to reduce the risk of undertreating pain. Opioid dosing for acute pain should be tailored to the patient with consideration of their baseline opioid therapy and previous effective therapy. The dose of opioids needed to manage acute pain will vary according to the patient and may be higher than standard doses prescribed for postoperative pain. Harm reduction strategies for chronic opioid therapy include co-prescribing naloxone and prescribing the lowest effective opioid dose. Morphine milligram equivalents (MME) should be documented. Many online MME calculators exist, one of which is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Opioid Guideline Mobile App. The usefulness of “pain contracts” is not known, but a well-written patient agreement can help establish informed consent, improve adherence, and mitigate risk when initiating opioid therapy. Attention should be paid to the risk of bias when assessing the opioid needs of an individual with chronic pain conditions, and an addiction medicine consultation should be considered if there is a concern for the need to differentiate opioid use disorder from chronic pain needs. How should pregnant patients with sickle cell disease on opioid therapy be counseled regarding the risk of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome? Available evidence suggests that approximately 1 in 4 infants born to a mother with SCD will have neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS). In one series, 4 of 15 infants (27%) born to mothers with hemoglobin SS disease were diagnosed with NOWS. The risk factors included antepartum admission, VOC, and exchange transfusion. In another series, 5 of 23 mothers (22%) with SCD who received opioids and 4 of 15 mothers (27%) with SCD who received daily opioids had an infant with NOWS. Another review demonstrated that the risk of NOWS was associated with mean daily opioid dose; median maternal oral morphine doses were 416, 139, and 4 mg for infants with severe, mild, and no NOWS, respectively. Patients with SCD using opioids during pregnancy should be counseled about the risk of NOWS and should participate in shared decision-making about an opioid dosing strategy to balance neonatal risks with the adequacy of pain management to maintain their well-being. Infants exposed to opioids in utero should be monitored for signs and symptoms of NOWS. Prenatal consultation with pediatrics is encouraged to develop a monitoring and treatment plan. The Eat, Sleep, Console treatment model prioritizes infant comfort and family involvement in care and is associated with reduced length of hospital stay, exposure to pharmacologic agents, and overall cost of treatment. - Patients can be reassured that breastfeeding is beneficial for infants with NOWS. , What is the role of transfusion in pregnant patients with sickle cell disease? Of note, 3 types of transfusions are used in the care of patients with SCD: simple transfusions consisting of red cell transfusion only, manual exchanges consisting of manual phlebotomy before transfusion of 1 to 2 units of packed RBCs, and automated exchange transfusions, which consist of the simultaneous removal of the patient’s full blood volume with an infusion of blood products. Transfusions are indicated during pregnancy for acute complications of SCD, such as stroke and ACS. In a 1988 randomized controlled trial, prophylactic transfusions during pregnancy reduced the number of pain crises compared with transfusions only when medically indicated but did not change other key maternal and perinatal outcomes. Concerns were raised by the authors regarding risks of alloimmunization, iron overload, hospital admissions, and excess healthcare costs. A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of studies of prophylactic transfusion in pregnancy identified 12 studies with 1291 participants found a moderate to high risk of bias among included studies and found an association between prophylactic transfusion and reduction in maternal mortality, VOC, pulmonary complications, venous thromboembolism (VTE), pyelonephritis, perinatal mortality, neonatal death, and preterm birth. Practically speaking, there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine chronic transfusion therapy (CTT) for most pregnant patients with SCD; individualized consideration should be given to patients with more severe historical features, such as those receiving chronic transfusion before pregnancy and those with a history of stroke. , We suggest the use of prophylactic transfusions be individualized for high-risk patients with SCD in accordance with ASH guidelines and directed by a hematologist and maternal-fetal medicine subspecialist in shared decision-making with the patient (GRADE 2B). What are the risks and benefits of blood transfusion in pregnancy? Blood transfusions in high-resource countries are considered safe and have low rates of adverse outcomes. The benefits of CTT, as described in a randomized trial, included reduced frequency of pain crises. In addition, observational data consisting of a systematic review and meta-analysis found that CTT reduced maternal mortality, pulmonary complications, pulmonary embolism, pyelonephritis, perinatal mortality, and preterm birth. Risks of blood transfusion during pregnancy include those inherent to blood transfusions in all patients, plus added risks to the pregnant patient and the developing fetus. Specifically, transfused blood should be cytomegalovirus (CMV) negative to avoid fetal CMV infection. Additional risks of blood transfusion include iron overload and alloimmunization. Liver iron concentration monitoring and chelation therapy are indicated to prevent the adverse consequences of iron overload, which include fibrosis and cirrhosis. , For patients with alloimmunization, early communication with the local blood bank is important to ensure matched blood can be obtained if needed. Furthermore, the pregnant patient with antibodies associated with hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn should be managed according to national guidelines. , In addition, delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions (DHTRs) should remain on the differential diagnosis for a pregnant person with SCD who presents with pain and dark urine after a previous blood transfusion. The duration from red cell transfusion to DHTR can range from days to weeks and is typically, but not always, diagnosed by the identification of new antibodies on their antibody screen. Supportive care, steroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin are likely the best approaches to treat a pregnant person with SCD and DHTR. Avoiding blood transfusions is ideal, although this can be challenging in a person with a low hemoglobin level approaching delivery. Multidisciplinary planning is crucial in these challenging cases. MFM specialists should be vigilant to keep DHTR on the differential diagnosis as they manage patients with SCD in conjunction with a hematologist, preferably one who specializes in SCD. What is the role of disease-modifying therapy, including hydroxyurea, in the management of sickle cell disease? All individuals with SCD should be offered disease-modifying therapy at baseline. For individuals with a history of recurrent VOC, ACS, stroke, or other chronic organ complications, additional emphasis on disease-modifying therapy is needed. Hydroxyurea is the best-studied disease-modifying therapy in SCD, attenuating the number of VOC episodes and slowing the progression of end-organ disease. Chronic red cell transfusion is the only disease-modifying therapy proven to decrease the risk of ischemic stroke in patients with CNS vasculopathy. Newer therapies (L-glutamine, voxelotor, and crizanlizumab) remain inconclusive in their potential for long-term efficacy and lack data on use during pregnancy. Of these therapies, only CTT is considered safe in pregnancy. About these newer therapies, shared decision-making should help guide whether certain agents should be continued during pregnancy. Hydroxyurea has historically not been recommended in pregnancy primarily because of teratogenic effects found in animal models. - Although available data are limited, a thorough search did not locate any reported cases of individuals taking hydroxyurea for SCD who had an infant with a birth defect, , and a systematic review is ongoing. A 2022 retrospective study of 1788 pregnancies, among which 241 (16%) were conceived while on hydroxyurea, did not demonstrate independent associations between use during conception and adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, among patients with SCD using hydroxyurea during conception and continuing use during pregnancy, there were increased risks of miscarriage or stillbirth (OR, 2.21; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09–7.38) and increased risk of low birthweight (OR, 2.98; 95% CI, 1.09–7.38) among term infants, after adjustment for markers of disease severity.
